LESSONS.title: What an inference engine actually does
LESSONS.goal: A chatbot answer depends on the trained model, the inference engine that runs it and the service around them, and each of these controls different costs.
LESSONS.recall: What do you think happens between sending a prompt and seeing the first word?
LESSONS.predict: If two companies serve identical weights, must their speed and running cost be identical?
example: Your team fine-tunes a chatbot, starts processing several users’ requests together and adds a sign-in page. Each change touches a different part of the system.

Fine-tuning the model so its replies follow your house style changes the learned weights, or a learned adapter on top of them. It belongs to the model, because the same input can now produce a different prediction.
Processing several people’s questions together leaves the weights exactly as they were. It is an engine decision about how the work is scheduled and executed.

The sign-in page, and sending each request to whichever machine is free, belong to the surrounding service. If the chatbot gets slower after a release, the part that changed is the first place to look.

questions.prompt: Two teams use exactly the same learned model weights. Could their engines still take different amounts of time and memory to answer?
options: No. Matching weights force identical execution costs.
Yes. The software can organize and execute the same calculations differently.
Only if one team retrains the model.
questions.why: Fixing the learned numbers leaves open how requests are grouped, how memory is managed and how each calculation runs. One engine may avoid repeated work that another engine performs.
questions.hint: Separate learned numbers from how they are executed.
option_feedback: Weights fix what is computed. How requests are grouped, how memory is managed and which kernels run are separate choices.
Correct. The same calculations can be scheduled, batched and executed in different ways, at different cost.
Retraining changes the weights, but the question holds them fixed, and execution cost can still differ.

questions.prompt: DeepInfer’s public release runs offline inference. What follows?
options: It is already a complete hosted chat service
It cannot allocate any KV memory
A service still needs surrounding components
questions.why: Offline execution keeps KV memory locally for each request. A hosted service would also need a cache shared across machines, live request routing and the other pieces that DeepInfer’s README lists as outside the release.
questions.hint: Each request’s own attention memory is different from a cache service shared by a fleet of machines.
option_feedback: A hosted chat service also needs routing, sign-in and streaming, which the release leaves out.
Every request needs local KV memory to run attention at all. What the release leaves out is a KV-cache service shared across machines.
Correct. The release covers execution, so routing, a shared cache service and the rest of a service must come from elsewhere.

transfer: A friend asks: “If the model has already been trained, why do we still need an inference engine?” Explain the difference, then name one job the surrounding service does.
Names weights and execution separately
Explains iterative next-token prediction
Names one surrounding service responsibility

Training produced the weights, the learned numbers that determine the model’s calculations. Answering repeats one loop. The engine runs those calculations, chooses a next token, appends it to the text so far and goes again. Along the way it manages memory and coordinates the many requests sharing the hardware. The surrounding service has its own jobs, such as signing users in and sending each request to an available machine.
LESSONS.takeaway: The model’s weights fix which calculations happen, and the inference engine decides how the hardware carries them out.

levels.1:
When you send a message to a chatbot there is a pause, and then the answer appears a few words at a time. Somewhere a computer is turning your message into that answer, and a different company running what looks like the same model may do it faster or more cheaply. People tend to call all of this “the model”, but three separate parts are involved, the learned model itself, the software that runs it and the service you actually talk to, and each of them can make the answer slower or faster for its own reasons.

During training, a computer adjusts an enormous collection of numbers until the model gets better at predicting text, and those numbers, saved to files at the end, are the model’s weights. You can think of them as the settings of a very large machine, whose values decide how information flows through it and which predictions come out. Fine-tuning changes those numbers, or adds a smaller learned update on top of them, which is why a fine-tuned model behaves differently from the one it started from.

Running the model to answer a question is called inference. The model scores every piece of text that could come next, one piece is picked and appended to the text so far, and the model scores again from the longer text. A response is that loop repeated until it stops. The weights stay fixed the whole time, so although the model’s working state grows as the conversation grows, nothing it learned changes after each word.

Something has to load the weights, reserve memory, decide which requests to work on together, run the calculations and keep track of every unfinished answer. That software is the inference engine, and it is where two deployments of identical weights can differ most, in how much memory they use and in how long they take.

Around the engine sits a service that signs you in, picks which machine receives your request and streams the answer back to your screen. Each of those steps adds its own delay, so a fast engine behind a slow service still feels slow.

The rest of the course studies DeepInfer, the inference engine that the AI company DeepSeek released as open source and describes in its DeepInfer README. Its choices about memory, batching and kernels make sense only once you know how tokens, attention and GPU memory behave, so the next few lessons cover those first.
levels.2:
It helps to follow one call through DeepInfer. A Python program starts it with LLM.generate, defined in the entry-point file deepinfer/entrypoints/llm.py. For each prompt, the helper _add_request copies the sampling settings and turns the text into token IDs, the integers that stand for pieces of text, using the Hugging Face tokenizer’s encode unless you passed token IDs yourself. It stores them as a NumPy int32 array and hands them to LLMEngine.add_request. No GPU has done anything yet, and the request is just a sequence object waiting in a queue.

From there _run_engine loops, calling LLMEngine.step() in the engine loop file deepinfer/engine/llm_engine.py for as long as any request is unfinished and collecting whatever each step produced. When everything is done it turns each request’s token IDs back into text with the tokenizer’s decode. Because one step advances every scheduled request by one round of the model, a 500-token answer takes hundreds of steps, interleaved with the steps that serve everyone else. (A later lesson on speculative decoding shows how one step can emit several tokens for the same request.)

Each step begins in the scheduler, written in C++ in csrc/engine/scheduler.hpp, which picks the sequences that run and decides whether this step processes prompts or extends answers. It also hands out blocks of KV cache, the memory where the engine keeps each request’s saved attention state (a later lesson explains it), and when blocks run out it preempts a sequence, pausing it and freeing its blocks. The plan then goes through _execute_model_async_step to the worker processes that drive the GPUs. Their execute_model_step in deepinfer/worker/worker.py builds the input tensors, runs the forward pass through all of the model’s layers, usually by replaying a recorded CUDA graph, and calls the sampler to pick each next token. Finally post_process folds the sampled tokens back into the sequences, marks the finished ones and returns RequestOutput records.

Most of the memory budget is settled before the first step. The workers load the weights, and profile_run then pushes a dummy batch of the largest configured size through the model to measure its peak working memory. Whatever is left goes to attention state, which deepinfer/worker/base.py computes as total memory times gpu_memory_utilization (0.9 by default), minus the profiled peak, minus a fixed area for per-sequence state, and then divides into cache blocks. On an invented 80 GB device holding 40 GB of weights with a 6 GB peak, that leaves about 72 − 40 − 6 = 26 GB for cached tokens. So raising max_num_seqs or the per-step token budget is not free, because the bigger profiling batch raises the peak and leaves fewer blocks for the requests themselves.

The engine’s interface shows where its job ends. It takes token IDs plus a SamplingParams object (temperature, top-p, top-k, maximum tokens, a seed, an optional grammar) and returns per-step records holding a token ID, its log probability and speculative-acceptance counts. Converting API requests, applying the chat template that formats a conversation for the model and streaming text to a browser all happen before encoding or after decoding, outside this loop, and DeepSeek ships that work separately. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production describes DeepSeek Recipe, a separate tool that turns Chat Completions, Responses and Messages requests (the request formats of the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs) into token sequences and parses the output back.

The README also lists what a full service needs beyond this release, which runs offline inference, meaning a script submits a fixed set of prompts and collects the results. A live service would add a KV cache system shared across machines, load balancing across data-parallel replicas (identical engine copies that split the traffic), and disaggregated deployment, in which vision encoding, prefill (processing the prompt) and decode (generating the answer) run on separate machines. You can see in the code where those pieces would attach. EngineType in deepinfer/engine/engine_type.py has NORMAL, PROMPT (prefill only) and COMPLETION (decode only), and the scheduler refuses to let a decode-only engine recompute a preempted request because that engine has no way to run a prompt. An offline run uses NORMAL, one engine doing both kinds of work.

Knowing the layers tells you where a symptom comes from. A mismatched tokenizer produces valid-looking IDs that the weights were never trained on, which is why the tokenizer loader, deepinfer/hugging_face/tokenizer.py, refuses to start unless the begin, end and padding tokens sit at IDs 0, 1 and 2. Too little memory headroom fails at startup with “No available memory for the cache blocks”, or shows up later as preemption. A scheduling choice, by contrast, changes latency without changing any number the model computes.

LESSONS.title: The math you need, without the fog
LESSONS.goal: Inference explanations rely on a small amount of arithmetic, mainly array shapes, matrix products, byte counts and transfer times.
LESSONS.recall: What is a weight, and what changes during inference?
LESSONS.predict: Does a vector with 4 entries multiplied by a 4×6 matrix produce 4 numbers or 6?
example: DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production gives the size of the sliding-window attention state it saves for each sequence as 20 layers × 134 tokens × 528 bytes. Where does each factor come from, and what does the total tell you?

The first two factors are a shape. The state covers 20 layers, and for each layer it keeps 134 recent positions: a 128-token window plus 6 spare positions so speculative decoding can back up a few tokens. That is 20 × 134 = 2,680 slots, whatever the values inside them are.

The third factor comes from the number format. Each slot holds 512 numbers in 8-bit FP8 plus one 1-byte scale per 32 numbers, so 512 + 16 = 528 bytes. Multiplying gives 1,415,040 bytes, about 1.4 MB per sequence. Because the window is fixed, that figure stays the same for a 1,000-token chat and a 100,000-token document.

The Q&A budgets 400 Gbps of network bandwidth per 8-GPU machine. Gbps counts bits, so that is 50 GB per second, or about 6.25 GB/s for each GPU’s share. At that share 1.4 MB moves in roughly 0.23 milliseconds, which is why the system can afford to fetch this state from another machine on a cache hit. Capacity says the state fits somewhere, and bandwidth says how long it takes to arrive.

questions.prompt: X has shape [8,4] and W has shape [4,6]. What shape is XW?
questions.why: The shared inner dimension 4 is summed away and the outer dimensions remain, so XW has 8 rows and 6 columns.
questions.hint: Put tokens on the rows and output features on the columns.
option_feedback: Correct. The shared inner dimension 4 is summed away, leaving the 8 rows of X and the 6 columns of W.
This keeps the inner dimension, which is exactly the one the multiplication combines.
[6,8] is the shape of the transpose, (XW)ᵀ. XW keeps the rows of X first.

questions.prompt: A model has a billion parameters stored at 2 bytes each, so its weights take 2 GB. A GPU has 2.5 GB free. Is that enough to serve the model?
options: Yes, with 0.5 GB to spare, because the weights are the whole footprint
Not necessarily, because the KV cache, activations and runtime overhead come on top and grow with requests and context
No, because each parameter needs 2 bytes for the weight and 2 more for its gradient
questions.why: Parameter count times bytes per parameter measures the weights only. Serving also holds each request’s attention cache, the intermediate activations of a step and the runtime’s own buffers, and the cache grows with the number of requests and their length.
questions.hint: What else does a running engine keep in memory besides the weights?
option_feedback: The 2 GB covers the weights alone. The cache for even a few long requests can take more than the remaining 0.5 GB.
Right. 2 GB is the weights only, and whether 0.5 GB is enough for everything else depends on how many requests run and how long they are.
Gradients exist only during training. Inference keeps the weights, but adds caches and working memory instead.

transfer: Explain the difference between how much memory a device has and how quickly it can move data. Use a small example.
Separates capacity from transfer rate
Names bytes/s as bandwidth
Explains why both constrain inference

Capacity is how much data fits at once, and bandwidth is how many bytes can move per second. DeepSeek’s saved sliding-window state is about 1.4 MB per sequence, and a storage server can hold millions of those. Holding them says nothing about how quickly one reaches a GPU. Over each GPU’s 6.25 GB/s share of the network it takes about a quarter of a millisecond. Inference needs both: room for the weights and caches, and enough bandwidth to bring them to the arithmetic units every step.
LESSONS.takeaway: A tensor’s shape says how many numbers it holds and how they are arranged, and units such as bytes and bytes per second say what a calculation measures.

levels.1:
Explanations of inference talk about “tensors” and “matrix multiplication” without stopping to define them, but the ideas are concrete enough to work through on paper. A vector is an ordered list of numbers, such as [2, 3], and a matrix is a rectangular table of them with rows and columns. Tensor is the general name for an array laid out along any number of directions, so a vector is a tensor with one direction and a matrix is one with two.

Suppose you have four requests, each ten text positions long, and you describe every position with six numbers. All of it fits in a tensor of shape [4, 10, 6], where the shape records how many requests, positions and features there are and says nothing about the values inside. That gap matters when you debug, because two tensors can share a shape and hold completely different values, so a passing shape check rules out some mistakes without telling you whether the model computed the right answer.

Most of a model’s work is multiplying by matrices. The basic piece is a dot product, which multiplies matching entries and adds them up, so [2, 3] · [4, 5] is 2 × 4 + 3 × 5 = 23. Matrix multiplication does many dot products at once, and inside a model a learned matrix uses them to turn one set of features into another. Papers write the shapes with symbols such as [B, d], where B might be the number of positions being processed and d the number of features per position. Multiplying that by a matrix of shape [d, h] gives [B, h], because the shared d is the dimension that gets summed away.

The other arithmetic that keeps coming up is about bytes, how many fit and how long they take to move. If each stored number takes two bytes, a billion numbers take two billion bytes, or two gigabytes, and that covers only those numbers, with any working memory on top. A device that moves a hundred gigabytes per second needs at least a hundredth of a second, ten milliseconds, to move one of those gigabytes. Capacity is how much fits and bandwidth is how fast it moves, and later lessons use that difference to explain why very fast hardware sometimes spends its time waiting.
levels.2:
Engines are consistent about how they lay these shapes out in memory. Activations, the intermediate values computed while the model runs, are stored row by row as [tokens, features], and a weight that maps d inputs to h outputs is stored as [h, d], one row per output. DeepInfer’s ReplicatedLinear in deepinfer/model_executor/layers/linear.py documents its weight as (output_size, input_size), and the routine that multiplies by it is bf16_gemm_nt, a BF16 GEMM (general matrix multiplication) that uses the first operand as stored and the second transposed. The last step of the model, which produces logits, a score for every possible next token, works the same way. In sampler_utils.get_logits, hidden states [tokens, d] times an embedding matrix stored as [vocab, d] give logits [tokens, vocab].

Work is counted in floating-point operations, FLOPs, with each multiply-add counting as two. Multiplying X[B,d] by a weight that maps d to h produces B×h outputs, each a sum of d products, so it costs about 2Bdh FLOPs. Added up over a whole model, a forward pass costs roughly 2N FLOPs per token for N parameters, plus an attention term that grows with context length. DeepInfer’s csrc/engine/flops_estimator.hpp counts the large matrix products the same way and leaves out small arithmetic such as normalizations, and the engine uses the total to report utilization, the share of the GPU’s peak arithmetic rate it actually reaches.

Bytes depend on the number format. A float32 value takes 4 bytes, and BF16 takes 2 by keeping float32’s range and giving up precision, down to about three significant decimal digits. The FP8 format E4M3 takes one byte and tops out at 448, and FP4 E2M1 takes half a byte and can represent only 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4 and 6, with a sign. Formats that narrow are usable only with block scaling, where a group of values shares one scale factor and each stored number is a small multiple of it.

DeepInfer’s KV cache, the attention state it saves for each earlier token (explained two lessons from now), shows these sizes at work. V41_FORMAT in tilelang_ops/cache_common.py stores, for each token and layer, 512 numbers in E4M3 plus one scale per 32 numbers in UE8M0, an unsigned 8-bit exponent that encodes a power of two. That comes to 512 + 16 = 528 bytes, against 1,024 for the same numbers in BF16. The FP4 variant, V41_FP4_FORMAT, packs two values per byte with one E4M3 scale per 16 values, for 256 + 32 = 288 bytes. Multiply by layers and tokens and you have a request’s cache footprint, with the weights, the activation peak and the runtime’s own buffers on top.

Since capacity is measured in bytes and bandwidth in bytes per second, dividing one by the other gives a time. Some sizes are easy to overlook until you multiply them out, and logits are one of them. DeepInfer’s tokenizer implies a vocabulary of 129,280 entries (its extra tokens start at that ID), so one float32 row of logits is 129,280 × 4 = 517,120 bytes, and a step that scores 256 positions writes about 132 MB of them before any sampling happens.

Probabilities are handled as logarithms, because multiplying many probabilities below one quickly underflows to zero while adding their logs does not (log(p₁p₂) = log p₁ + log p₂). A model’s quality on known text is reported as its average negative log probability per token, and the exponential of that average is perplexity. DeepInfer’s offline example script, examples/offline_inference.py, computes it for each generated answer as exp(−sum(logps) / len(logps)).

LESSONS.title: Tokens, logits and choosing what comes next
LESSONS.goal: A model produces a response by repeatedly scoring every possible next token, choosing one and appending it to the text.
LESSONS.recall: How is a probability different from an arbitrary numerical score?
LESSONS.predict: If you raise temperature, do you add knowledge or change how the same scores are sampled?
example: The model gives three possible next tokens probabilities of 66.5%, 24.5% and 9%. What happens next?
Under greedy decoding the engine picks the first token, because 66.5% is the largest probability. No random draw is needed.

Under sampling the first token is still the most likely, but either of the others can be drawn. Seeing the second token, which has a 24.5% chance, is no evidence on its own that the engine made a mistake.

Whichever token is chosen joins the sequence, and the next prediction uses the updated sequence. Raising the temperature would reshape the distribution for this choice and leave the learned weights untouched.

questions.prompt: What does temperature change?
options: The learned weights
The next-token sampling distribution
The tokenizer vocabulary
questions.why: Temperature rescales the logits at sampling time, after the model has computed them. The weights and the vocabulary stay as they were.
questions.hint: Which part happens after the model computes its scores?
option_feedback: Temperature is applied after the model has produced its scores, and the weights that produced them stay fixed.
Correct. Dividing the logits by T reshapes the probabilities used to pick the next token.
The vocabulary is fixed by the tokenizer. Temperature only changes how likely each existing token is to be picked.

questions.prompt: Why can’t ordinary autoregressive generation choose 100 unknown future tokens independently in one step?
options: Each choice conditions later predictions
All GPUs forbid matrices with 100 rows
Tokenization is random
questions.why: Each future conditional distribution depends on the tokens generated before it. Speculative decoding works around this by proposing several candidates and then verifying them.
questions.hint: The prompt is already known, and the answer is not.
option_feedback: Correct. The distribution for each token depends on which tokens were chosen before it, so later choices cannot be made first.
GPUs routinely multiply matrices with far more than 100 rows. The limit comes from the dependency between tokens.
Tokenization is deterministic for a given tokenizer. Randomness enters only at sampling.

questions.prompt: Two engines produce different text from the 20th generated token onward. Which check comes next?
options: Only compare the final paragraphs
Teacher-force the same prefixes and compare logits
Increase temperature until the text looks similar
questions.why: Once two outputs diverge, every later token is conditioned on a different history. Teacher forcing keeps the history identical, so any remaining difference in logits comes from the computation itself.
questions.hint: Keep the input to the comparison identical.
option_feedback: The final paragraphs mix every earlier difference together and cannot show where the first disagreement began.
Correct. Feeding both engines the same prefixes lets you compare their scores before different histories confound the comparison.
Raising temperature buries the disagreement under more randomness and makes the outputs harder to compare.

transfer: Explain how a model goes from a prompt to a longer answer. Include where choosing the next token happens.
Describes turning text into token IDs
Explains scoring, choosing, and appending a next token
Explains why the chosen token affects the next prediction

The tokenizer turns the prompt into token IDs. The model computes a score for every possible next token, and the engine’s selection rule picks one. That token is appended before the next prediction, so each choice shapes the input to the next step. The tokenizer and stop markers have to match what the model was trained with. Changing temperature changes which tokens get picked, while the learned weights stay the same.
LESSONS.takeaway: Generation repeatedly scores the possible next tokens, chooses one with a sampling rule, and adds it to the text before the next prediction.

levels.1:
Before the model runs, a piece of software called the tokenizer breaks your text into pieces and gives each one an integer. The pieces are tokens and the integers are token IDs. A token can be a common word, part of a word, a punctuation mark or a special marker, so an invented tokenizer might split “unhelpful” into “un”, “help” and “ful”, while a real one makes its own choices.

That is why a limit of a thousand tokens is a different limit from a thousand words, and why a fine-tuned model has to be loaded with its own tokenizer. Its weights were learned against those particular IDs, and a different tokenizer would hand it numbers that mean something else.

Suppose the input ends with “The sky is”. The model produces a score for every token it could place next, with some continuations scoring far higher than others. These raw scores are called logits, and because they need not add up to one they are not yet probabilities. A function called softmax turns them into probabilities, which say how likely each candidate is and do sum to one across all of them.

The engine still has to pick one. It can take the highest-scoring token every time, which is called greedy decoding, or it can draw a token at random according to the probabilities. With random drawing a less likely token is sometimes chosen, in the same way that a coin landing heads 70% of the time still lands tails now and then.

Temperature controls how concentrated those probabilities are. At a low temperature the top choices take more of the probability, and at a high temperature it spreads over more candidates. The model’s knowledge is untouched either way, since only the rule for choosing has changed.

Once a token is chosen, the engine appends it to the sequence and the model scores what could follow the longer text. Choosing “blue” puts the model in a different situation from choosing “clear”, so every later prediction can differ. The cycle of scoring, choosing and appending repeats until a stopping condition, such as a special end-of-answer token or a length limit, and the answer on your screen is the sequence of tokens chosen along the way.
levels.2:
Softmax with temperature T turns logits z into probabilities pᵢ = exp(zᵢ/T) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ/T). With three candidates whose logits are 2, 1 and 0, T = 1 gives exponentials of 7.39, 2.72 and 1, which sum to 11.11, so the probabilities are 66.5%, 24.5% and 9.0%. Halving the temperature to 0.5 doubles the scaled logits to 4, 2 and 0 and sharpens the probabilities to 86.7%, 11.7% and 1.6%, while T = 2 flattens them to 50.6%, 30.7% and 18.6%. The model produced the same three logits every time, and only the selection step changed.

In DeepInfer the logits come from get_logits in deepinfer/model_executor/layers/sampler_utils.py, which multiplies the final hidden states by the embedding matrix into a float32 tensor of shape [tokens, vocab]. The Sampler class in the DeepInfer sampler file first keeps only the rows that need a choice. During a prompt pass that is the last prompt position of each request, since every other prompt position already has a known next token.

The order of the selection steps is easiest to read in fused_sample_ref, the plain PyTorch version of the GPU kernel in tilelang_ops/fused_sample.py. If the environment variable DEEPINFER_SAMPLER_FORCE_TOPK is set (the offline example uses 4,096), only the 4,096 highest logits survive. Those are divided by T, then top-p removes every candidate whose preceding cumulative probability already exceeds p, top-k removes everything ranked below k, and a log-softmax renormalizes what is left. With the T = 1 numbers above and p = 0.9, the first two tokens survive because the probability before the second is only 0.665, and the third goes because 0.91 precedes it. An engine that applies the same settings in a different order can keep a different set of tokens, so comparing two engines means checking the order as well as the settings.

Greedy decoding has no separate code path. SamplingParams in deepinfer/sampling_params.py raises any temperature below 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁵ and switches off top-p and top-k, and at that temperature a logit gap of 0.01 becomes a factor of e¹⁰⁰⁰ in probability, so the highest-scoring token wins except on exact ties.

The random draw is built to be reproducible. random_sampling_ref in tilelang_ops/random_sampling.py hashes the request’s 64-bit seq_seed together with the token’s position (using SplitMix64, a standard integer hash) into a uniform number u between 0 and 1, then returns the first token whose cumulative probability, summed in float64, exceeds u times the total. Because u depends only on the seed and the position, a request’s draw does not change with batch size or row order. If you pass no seed, SamplingParams picks a random one and runs will differ.

Stopping is decided at the same point. A request ends when it emits the end-of-sequence token (ID 1 for this tokenizer), unless ignore_eos is set, or when it reaches max_tokens, which defaults to 16. Setting a token’s logit to −∞ before sampling removes it from the draw, and the engine uses that one trick for several jobs. The prefill path uses it to forbid the end token as the first output (first_n_token_no_eos), and structured outputs, which force the answer to follow a grammar such as a JSON schema, use it at every step, where a grammar matcher produces a bitmask of legal tokens and every other logit is set to −∞.

None of this removes the sequential dependency. An autoregressive model factors a sequence’s probability as P(x₁…xₙ) = Πₜ P(xₜ | x<ₜ), so the distribution for position t is not even defined until the tokens before it have been chosen. Known prompt tokens can all be scored in one pass, but unknown ones must be chosen in order, or proposed in bulk and then checked, which is what speculative decoding does.
levels.3:
Token boundaries are also a security boundary. Control tokens are the special tokens that mark who is speaking or where the model’s reasoning ends, and a user who could type one could make their text look like part of the conversation’s structure. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production says DeepSeek Recipe, its tool for formatting requests, encodes a literal <｜User｜> typed by a user as ordinary text tokens and recognizes the end-of-reasoning marker only by its token ID, so typed text cannot impersonate either. The same exactness matters when comparing engines, since a comparison means nothing until both produce identical token IDs for the input.

Some engine shortcuts change the distribution being sampled. DeepInfer’s force_topk gives zero probability to every token outside the top 4,096, and while the probability it removes is usually tiny, it is never exactly zero and it grows at high temperature. DeepInfer’s distribution test, tests/models/test_kl.py, accounts for this by refusing any nonzero tolerance on KL divergence while force_topk is on, because a token with zero probability in one distribution and positive probability in the other makes the divergence infinite. Grammar masks shift the distribution too. Kanghee Park and colleagues showed in 2024 that masking token by token does not sample from the model’s distribution restricted to grammatical outputs, and fast mask libraries such as Yixin Dong and colleagues’ XGrammar, which DeepInfer uses, do not remove that bias.

Reproducibility takes more than a seed. A seed fixes the random draws, but the logits themselves can shift by a rounding error when a kernel sums in a different order, for example because the batch grew. Horace He’s 2025 essay for Thinking Machines Lab traced most run-to-run nondeterminism in served models to this lack of batch invariance. DeepInfer deals with both causes, since its sampler keys the random number to seed and position and DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 makes kernels compute the same result whatever else is in the batch. Even so, the README requires DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=0 for deterministic sampling, because with that setting on the engine decides from the current load how many speculative draft tokens to verify, and that changes which random draws get consumed.

When two engines produce different text anyway, comparing their scores locates the cause better than comparing the text, since after the first differing token each engine is continuing a different history. Teacher forcing avoids that by feeding both engines the same continuation and comparing log probabilities at identical prefixes. DeepInfer supports it through golden_token_ids in SamplingParams. In the sampler, _update_golden_tokens replaces each sampled token with the given one while still recording the model’s log probability for it, and the first position where the two engines’ log probabilities differ by more than rounding noise is where to start looking.

LESSONS.title: A transformer pass and its KV cache
LESSONS.goal: Attention lets each new token draw on earlier text, and the engine keeps earlier keys and values in a KV cache so it does not have to recompute them.
LESSONS.recall: What makes a generated token depend on earlier ones?
LESSONS.predict: If you retain old keys and values, do you still need to compare a new query with them?
example: The prompt contains tokens A, B and C, and the engine is now processing token D. What can it reuse?
The engine already holds keys and values for A, B and C at every layer. They stay in this request’s cache, and D’s arrival is no reason to rebuild them.

Compute D’s query, key and value. D’s query is compared with every visible key, including D’s own, and the matching values are mixed into D’s attention result. The engine reads the earlier cache to do this.

Append D’s key and value so the next position can use them. If the engine reads another request’s cache by mistake, or writes D into the wrong slot, the result can be wrong even though the cache has the expected length.

questions.prompt: What does a KV cache mainly save?
options: Recomputing earlier positions’ keys and values
All future attention calculations
The need for model weights
questions.why: Each new query still attends to the cached context. What the cache saves is rebuilding the earlier positions’ keys and values at every step.
questions.hint: Skipping a recomputation is different from skipping the reads.
option_feedback: Correct. Keys and values for earlier positions are computed once and read again, instead of being recomputed.
Each new query still has to attend over the cached keys and values. The cache saves recomputation, and the reads remain.
The cache holds per-request intermediate results. The weights are still needed to compute every new position.

questions.prompt: Can a text token reuse the same KV vector in any sentence?
options: Yes, keys depend only on spelling
No, hidden states depend on context and position
Only if temperature is zero
questions.why: Later-layer representations reflect the preceding tokens and the token’s position, so a key or value is tied to one history.
questions.hint: The token embedding is only the start of the computation.
option_feedback: Spelling fixes only the token’s embedding. Keys and values at later layers depend on the preceding text and the position.
Correct. Hidden states reflect the preceding tokens and the position, so the same token gets different keys and values in different contexts.
Temperature affects only how the next token is chosen and has no effect on the keys and values the layers compute.

questions.prompt: Which check most directly tests a KV cache?
options: Generated output looks fluent
Full-forward and incremental logits agree on the same prefixes
The cache has the expected Python type
questions.why: Numerical agreement across positions tests the actual computation the cache is meant to reproduce.
questions.hint: Which option compares the cached computation with one that does not use the cache?
option_feedback: Fluent text can hide a subtly wrong cache, because the model may still produce plausible words from slightly wrong scores.
Correct. If incremental and full-forward logits match at every prefix, the cache reproduces the computation it replaces.
A correct Python type says nothing about whether the stored values are the right ones.

transfer: Walk through what the engine does when one new token arrives. What does it calculate, and what can it reuse?
Computes a new query/key/value
Uses past keys and values
Appends request-specific state

The new position needs its own query, key and value. Its query is compared with the visible keys to decide how to mix the matching values. Keys and values for earlier positions come from this request’s cache and are not recalculated. The engine then appends the new key and value to that cache. It still reads the earlier state on every step, and that state has to come from the correct history.
LESSONS.takeaway: The engine saves each earlier position’s keys and values so a new token can attend to them without recomputing them, though it still reads them at every step.

levels.1:
Read “The trophy would not fit in the suitcase because it was too large.” To work out what “it” refers to you have to use words elsewhere in the sentence. A model faces the same problem, so the representation at one position needs a way to draw on information from other positions, and transformers provide it with attention. The model first turns each token into a list of numbers called an embedding, then transforms and mixes those lists through a stack of layers, each one stage of the calculation.

At each position, a layer computes three lists of numbers called the query, key and value. The query is compared with the keys of every visible position to give matching scores, and those scores decide how much of each position’s value goes into a weighted mixture, so a position with a high score contributes more. The names suggest a database lookup, but all three are numbers produced by multiplying by learned matrices, named for the part each plays in that comparison.

A model trained to continue text must never see the token it is supposed to predict, so a causal mask blocks attention to later positions. That has a useful side effect for the engine. Since no position can see anything after it, the computation for earlier positions stays exactly the same when a new token is appended.

The engine can therefore reuse that work. Once it has processed “The sky is”, it already holds keys and values for those positions, and when it moves on to the next token it can keep them in memory instead of computing them again. This saved state is the KV cache, K for keys and V for values. The new position still needs its own calculations, and its query still has to read every saved key and value, so caching removes repeated work while the earlier context is still read on every step.

Each cached entry belongs to one place in one text. “Bank” in a sentence about a river ends up with a different representation from “bank” in a sentence about money, because deeper layers fold in context, so a key or value cannot be reused just because the same token ID turns up somewhere else. The engine has to keep the right state for each request, use it in the right order and release it once it is no longer needed, and if it mixes up requests or positions the predictions go wrong while every array still has a valid shape.
levels.2:
Written with shapes, one attention head with head size dₕ computes Q = XW_q, K = XW_k and V = XW_v, each [tokens, dₕ], and outputs softmax(QKᵀ/√dₕ + M)V. M holds 0 for visible pairs and −∞ for hidden ones, which gives hidden pairs zero weight, and dividing by √dₕ keeps the dot products from growing with head size. Many heads run in parallel with their own projections, and an output projection mixes their results. Positions enter through rotary embeddings (RoPE), which rotate each query and key by an angle set by its position before the dot product, so a cached key is already rotated for the position it came from.

Conventional multi-head attention stores a key and a value for every head in every layer, which costs 2 × heads × dₕ × bytes per token per layer. For an invented model with 32 layers and 32 heads of size 128 in BF16, that is 2 × 32 × 128 × 2 = 16,384 bytes per layer, 512 KiB per token across all layers and 2 GiB for a single 4,096-token conversation, and generating each new token reads all of it again. It is usually the cache, growing with every conversation and every token, that limits how many conversations fit on one device.

DeepInfer’s V4.1 attention, in deepinfer/model_executor/models/v4_modules/attn.py, shrinks that figure in several ways at once. All heads share one 512-number latent per token, a design called multi-head latent attention (MLA), so the prompt-processing kernel receives keys shaped [total_k, 1, head_dim] instead of one per head. The latent is stored in FP8 with block scales at 528 bytes per token per layer, about 31 times smaller than the 16 KiB example. Some layers keep only a sliding window of recent tokens, while others keep a compressed cache in which each entry summarizes several tokens (kv_compress_ratio), and a small indexer in index_attn.py scores those entries and passes each query only the top-scoring ones. What a query can see is therefore a list of indices, which generalizes the triangular causal mask.

Prefill, the pass that processes a whole prompt at once, and decode, which adds one generated token per step, call different kernels in deepinfer/model_executor/layers/attention_backend.py. In prefill, forward assembles one buffer of keys from the cached window, the window keys computed in this pass and compressed entries loaded from the paged cache (which stores entries in fixed-size blocks), and then calls prefill_attn_varlen_sparse. “Varlen” means sequences of different lengths are packed end to end in one [total_q, heads, dim] tensor instead of each being padded to a common length. In decode, decode_mla_mqa_sparse reads straight from the paged cache, which is laid out as raw bytes in [num_blocks, block_size, 1, bytes_per_token], following each query’s index list.

Ordering bugs tend to show up where the cache is written. New keys pass through one fused kernel, fused_norm_rope_hadamard_cast_store_kvcache, which normalizes, applies RoPE, rotates, casts to FP8 and stores, and the store location comes from a slot mapping that translates each token position into a block and an offset within it. A comment in attn.py warns that the window’s store slots can overlap the ranges just loaded, so prefill must store only after the cache load. If the two were reversed, the kernel would read values it had just overwritten and produce wrong output with every shape still correct.

Because a cache entry depends on the layer, the position and every token before it, two requests that share a prompt prefix can share those entries. That is the basis of prefix caching, and DeepInfer’s scheduler copies block tables when a request forks. The same token ID at a different position, or after different text, gets a different entry.
levels.3:
Most of the history of attention in inference is about shrinking the cache. Noam Shazeer’s 2019 multi-query attention let all heads share one key and value, cutting the cache by the head count at some cost in quality, and Joshua Ainslie and colleagues’ grouped-query attention (GQA, 2023) settled in between with one key-value pair per group of heads. The DeepSeek-V2 paper (2024) went further with multi-head latent attention, which compresses keys and values into a low-rank latent and reconstructs each head’s view from it. It reported a 93.3% smaller KV cache and up to 5.76 times the generation throughput of DeepSeek 67B. DeepInfer’s single shared latent per token descends from that design, though the V2 paper does not describe V4.1 itself.

Another line of work limits which tokens a query can see. Longformer (Iz Beltagy and colleagues, 2020) and later Mistral 7B used sliding windows, and Guangxuan Xiao and colleagues’ StreamingLLM (2023) found that windowed attention breaks unless the first few tokens are kept, because models put large attention weight on them whatever they contain. DeepInfer passes a learned per-head attn_sink parameter to FlashMLA, DeepSeek’s attention kernels, for the same reason. DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp then let the model choose what each query sees, with a lightweight indexer that picks the top-k past entries, and DeepInfer’s index_attn.py describes its indexer the same way, computing relu(q @ k) * weights scores and keeping the top-k blocks.

A third approach shares the cache across layers. Yutao Sun and colleagues’ You Only Cache Once (2024) let later layers attend to keys and values produced once by earlier layers, and DeepInfer’s yoco.py and cross_layer.py split layers into producers and consumers in that spirit. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production describes an approximation built on top. Instead of rebuilding a consumer layer’s window over the last 2,560 tokens, prefill replays only the last 128, which the authors say nearly halves prefill computation. The result is used only for decoding and never enters the shared prefix cache, so an approximate entry cannot later be reused as if it were exact.

The memory each of these designs saves is exact arithmetic, but what it costs in quality has to be measured, and long-context measurements are weak. A model can retrieve one planted fact from a long document and still fail at tasks that combine many facts, and windows, compression, sparsity and replay each discard information differently, with errors that can compound over a long generation. Inside the engine there is a sharper check. tests/models/test_kl.py runs the same image-and-text inputs once step by step through decode and once as a single prefill over the prompt plus a known continuation, then compares log probabilities at every position with the allowed KL divergence set to zero. That catches a cache written to the wrong slot, a misaligned position or a stale window, all of which still produce fluent text. It cannot catch an approximation that both paths share, which is why the bounded replay is kept out of the comparison and out of the prefix cache.

LESSONS.title: Prefill, decode and what users feel
LESSONS.goal: The wait before an answer starts and the speed at which it continues come from different phases of work, prefill and decode, and are measured separately.
LESSONS.recall: Why are known prompt tokens different from unknown generated tokens?
LESSONS.predict: A huge prompt gives a long initial pause but fast streaming. Which phase should you investigate first?
example: DeepInfer can run prefill and decode on one engine, but DeepSeek’s production service runs them on separate machines. What goes wrong when they share, and what does the split change?

On a shared NORMAL engine every step is either all prefill or all decode. A new prompt waits until the data-parallel ranks vote for a prefill step, which they do only every 70 decode steps, and that wait counts toward its time to first token. When the prefill step runs, every answer already streaming pauses for it, so those users see one long gap.

In production, prefill runs on ordinary 8-GPU machines using the smallest expert-parallel size that memory allows, and decode runs on 64–128-GPU groups with the widest expert parallelism available. Each pool is sized for its own work: long prompts processed in parallel on one side, many sequences advancing one token at a time on the other. The Q&A says this lets time to first token and time between tokens be controlled independently.

The split has costs. Every request’s attention state has to cross the network from a prefill machine to a decode machine, and the two pools scale on different signals. Prefill adds machines according to the number of prompt tokens that missed the cache, and decode adds them according to the number of running requests.

questions.prompt: An answer begins after a long pause and then streams quickly. Which metric should you look at first?
options: TTFT
Only final token count
Training loss
questions.why: The symptom concerns the time until the first token, so TTFT is the measurement that matches it. The quick streaming suggests decode is not the problem.
questions.hint: Which metric covers the wait before anything appears?
option_feedback: Correct. The symptom is the wait before the first token, which is exactly what TTFT measures.
The token count says how long the answer is, and nothing about when its first token arrived.
Training loss describes how well the model learned. It says nothing about serving delay.

questions.prompt: DeepSeek scales its prefill machines by the number of prompt tokens that missed the cache, and its decode machines by the number of running requests. Why use different signals?
options: Prefill work grows with the prompt tokens it must compute, while decode work per step is set by how many sequences are generating
Prefill is cheaper than decode, so it needs a coarser signal
The two signals are interchangeable, and each team chose its own
questions.why: Prefill processes every uncached prompt token, so its load tracks those tokens. Decode advances each running sequence by one step at a time, so its load tracks how many sequences are active and how much cache they read.
questions.hint: What does each phase have to process per unit of time?
option_feedback: Right. Each phase is scaled by the quantity that drives its own work.
Neither phase is uniformly cheaper. The signals differ because the work in each phase grows with different things.
A burst of long prompts raises uncached tokens without adding running requests at first, so the two signals can move independently.

questions.prompt: DeepSeek reports that dynamic-length verification lowers estimated throughput by 1.5% at 16 concurrent sequences and raises it by 11% at 96, compared with always verifying five draft tokens. What best explains the difference?
options: The verification work it saves only matters once the GPU is saturated
The draft model guesses better when more sequences are running
At 96 sequences the engine runs prefill steps less often
questions.why: At light load the GPU has spare capacity, so trimming verification work frees nothing useful and the shorter checks cost a little output. At heavy load every verified token competes for saturated compute, so checking fewer unlikely tokens leaves room for other sequences.
questions.hint: When does saving work on a GPU turn into more output?
option_feedback: Correct. Saved work only raises throughput when the GPU was the limit, which happens at high concurrency.
The figures compare the same draft model at different loads. What changes is whether the GPU has spare capacity.
The comparison is between two verification policies on decode steps, and prefill scheduling is not what differs.

transfer: Someone says their chatbot is slow. What would you ask and measure before choosing a fix?
Separates initial delay and streaming gaps
Includes queueing/preprocessing
Requests workload and percentile measurements

I would first ask whether the delay comes before the first token or between later tokens. The initial wait can include queueing, input preparation and prompt processing. Later gaps point at continued generation, though delivery can matter there too. I would time those stages under the person’s real input lengths and request load, and look at the slow requests as well as the average. That tells me where to start.
LESSONS.takeaway: Prefill processes the known prompt in one pass and decode generates unknown tokens one step at a time, so the two use different resources and show up in different latency metrics.

levels.1:
You ask a question and wait several seconds before anything appears, and then the answer pours out. Another service starts answering almost at once and then trickles along. Both get described as “the model is slow”, but the two symptoms usually have different causes, because inference engines split the work into two kinds, prefill and decode.

Prefill processes the text that is already known, which is your prompt. Every prompt token is available before the model starts answering, so a well-organized engine can process many prompt positions together, as long as none of them reads ahead of itself. This pass builds the attention state that generation will reuse.

Decode produces the answer, whose tokens do not exist yet. The engine chooses one, feeds it back in and repeats, and that dependency on the previous choice makes decode behave very differently from prefill.

The two phases show up in different measurements. Time to first token (TTFT) is how long the first generated token takes to arrive, and a high TTFT can come from waiting in a queue, preparing the input, processing the prompt or delivering the result. Inter-token latency, also called time between tokens, is the gap between successive generated tokens once the answer has begun, which is what makes it flow smoothly or in fits.

Throughput measures something else again, the total work completed per second across all requests. A server answering a hundred people can post high throughput while each of them watches a slow answer, so any speed figure has to say whether it describes one user or the whole system.

If a long document produces a long initial pause and then fast streaming, prompt processing and everything before it are the first suspects, and if the first token comes quickly and the rest are slow, generation is. Queueing and network delays can produce either symptom, so these are only starting points. When you evaluate an engine for your own model you need both the initial wait and the streaming speed, since a single tokens-per-second figure leaves out the wait before the answer begins.
levels.2:
The two phases lean on different resources. Prefill over n prompt tokens multiplies every weight by n token vectors, so each byte of weight fetched from memory supports about n multiply-adds, and attention adds work that grows with n times the visible length. Decode runs one new position per request, so each weight byte supports only as many multiply-adds as there are requests in the batch, and every request’s cache has to be read again. A long prompt therefore tends to keep the arithmetic units busy while a small decode batch spends most of its time waiting on memory, which the next lesson works out in numbers.

That difference is also why throughput and per-user speed pull apart. If 64 requests each receive 30 tokens per second, each user sees 30 tokens per second and the system produces 64 × 30 = 1,920. Growing the batch usually raises the second number and lowers the first, because each step does more work and takes longer.

For diagnosis it helps to break TTFT into queue + preprocessing + prefill + first sample + delivery. After the first token, time per output token (TPOT) averages the remaining gaps as (end-to-end time − TTFT) / (output tokens − 1), while inter-token latency, ITL, is the whole distribution of individual gaps. TPOT is the mean of that distribution, but the slowest gaps, which a user notices as stutter, only appear in the distribution itself.

DeepInfer’s scheduler shows how an engine trades these off. In a NORMAL engine each step is entirely a prompt step or entirely a decode step, and SchedulerOutputs.prompt_run records which. The engine runs as several data-parallel ranks, copies that each handle part of the traffic, and all ranks must run the same kind of step together, so csrc/engine/scheduler.hpp makes decode the default and switches only by vote. Every 70 decode steps (DEEPINFER_PREFILL_ATTEMPT_INTERVAL) the ranks vote, and a prefill step happens only if every rank has a waiting prompt. Every 100 steps (DEEPINFER_PREFILL_ANY_ATTEMPT_INTERVAL) one rank with work is enough, and a rank declines to prefill while its KV cache is more than 90% full.

Those intervals have a price. With an invented 25 ms decode step, a prompt that arrives just after a prefill step can wait up to 70 steps, 1.75 s, before its prefill begins, or up to 2.5 s if no other rank has work. That wait is part of TTFT, and a timer around the model’s forward pass never sees it. When the prefill step does run, every in-flight answer pauses for it, so those users see one long gap. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production says the production deployment avoids both costs by running separate prefill and decode engines, the PROMPT and COMPLETION engine types.

Long prompts run into a per-step token budget, max_num_batched_tokens (32,768 in the offline example). Chunked prefill splits a longer prompt across several steps to fit, but it is off by default in EngineArgs, and without it a prompt over the budget is rejected. The Q&A describes a finer rule used in production, where each prefill step gets a time budget and a fitted cost model, quadratic in the number of new tokens and the length of the already-cached prefix, sets the largest chunk that fits.

Two more features change what the gaps look like. Asynchronous scheduling, on by default, has the CPU schedule step N+1 and post-process step N−1 while the GPU runs step N, so the GPU does not sit idle during bookkeeping. Speculative decoding, in which a cheap draft proposes several tokens and the model checks them together, lets a decode step emit several tokens per request. The Q&A reports about 3.2 accepted tokens per step at its operating point, so a 30 ms step averages about 9 ms per token, but the tokens arrive in bursts that show up in an ITL histogram.
levels.3:
Systems researchers have disagreed about how to schedule the two phases. Once Orca (Gyeong-In Yu and colleagues, OSDI 2022) let requests join and leave a batch at every iteration, prefill and decode began competing within the same steps, and a long prefill could pause every running answer. Amey Agrawal and colleagues’ Sarathi-Serve (OSDI 2024) called these pauses “generation stalls” and kept both phases on the same machines, splitting prompts into chunks and adding one chunk to each decode step, which accepts a slightly longer TTFT in exchange for steady gaps. Yinmin Zhong and colleagues’ DistServe and Pratyush Patel and colleagues’ Splitwise (both 2024) argued for putting the phases on different machines, each sized and parallelized for its own bottleneck, at the cost of moving the KV cache between them.

DistServe also changed how such systems are compared. It defines goodput as the highest request rate at which a target share of requests, say 90%, meet both a TTFT objective and a per-token objective, which is how a product team actually sets latency targets. Under that measure a configuration with higher peak throughput can come out worse if it misses the targets more often, and systems get compared at the same objectives instead of each at its own best point.

DeepInfer’s release sits on the disaggregated side of that argument. Its colocated NORMAL engine alternates whole prefill and decode steps by vote instead of mixing chunks into decode steps as Sarathi-Serve does. That keeps every step uniform across data-parallel ranks and makes batch invariance easier to achieve, but it accepts stalls and queueing whenever both phases share machines. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production says production sidesteps that by running prefill and decode on separate machines, at roughly one prefill GPU per decode GPU. The release ships the engine types for that split but not the load balancers that make it work, so an outside team running a single offline engine is measuring a different system from the one DeepSeek describes.

Load also changes which optimizations pay off. With dynamic-length speculative verification, the engine decides how many draft tokens to check from the draft’s confidence and the current load. The Q&A reports that, compared with always verifying five draft tokens, it changes estimated throughput per rank by −1.5% at 16 concurrent sequences, +5.4% at 60 and +11.0% at 96. It hurts at light load and helps at heavy load, because the verification work it saves only matters once the GPU is saturated. These are the authors’ estimates from their own benchmark data. Predicting prefill cost well enough to set chunk budgets is still hard, and nobody has agreed how to define goodput for agent workloads, where one task spans dozens of requests.

LESSONS.predict: If weights take 8 ms to read but arithmetic takes 1 ms, will twice the arithmetic speed halve the step?
example: In DeepSeek’s production decode, each step adds roughly one token per running sequence, and every MoE layer has to read the weights of each expert that received tokens. What limits that step, and what did DeepSeek change?

Each expert sees only the tokens routed to it, often a handful per step. Every weight byte fetched from HBM then supports only a few multiply-adds, so the arithmetic units spend most of the step waiting for data. Faster tensor cores would leave that waiting time where it was.

DeepSeek stores routed-expert weights in MXFP4, four-bit values with one shared power-of-two scale per 32. That is a little over half a byte per weight instead of BF16’s two, so reading the same experts moves roughly a quarter of the bytes. The saving is real only because the kernels consume the format directly, without first expanding it back to BF16.

Decode also runs across 64–128 GPUs with expert parallelism. Each GPU then holds only a few experts, about 7 at EP64, so it reads fewer weight bytes per step, and each expert collects tokens from the whole group, so each byte read does more work. DeepSeek’s Q&A gives the drop in per-step memory traffic as the reason this raises throughput.

questions.prompt: When do faster math units help least?
options: Memory movement dominates
Arithmetic dominates
The model has a name
questions.why: Speeding up a resource that is not the limit leaves the limiting cost in place. An operation that spends eight milliseconds fetching data and one millisecond computing would save at most that one millisecond even with infinitely fast arithmetic.
questions.hint: Compare the two time estimates.
option_feedback: Correct. When moving data takes longer than the arithmetic, faster arithmetic shortens a cost that was not setting the pace.
When arithmetic dominates, faster math units attack exactly the limiting cost, so this is where they help most.
A model’s name has no effect on execution. The answer depends on which resource is the limit.

questions.prompt: A small-batch decode step is limited by reading expert weights from HBM. DeepSeek stores those weights in MXFP4 instead of BF16. When does that shorten the step?
options: Whenever the format is used, by the full ratio of bytes saved
When the kernels read the narrow format directly, so fewer bytes actually cross from HBM
Never, because a number format only changes how much memory the weights occupy
questions.why: A memory-bound step takes about as long as its bytes take to arrive. A narrower format cuts those bytes only if the kernel consumes it as stored. A separate pass that expands the weights back to BF16 would add traffic and give some or all of the saving back.
questions.hint: Which resource sets the step’s pace, and does the format reduce it?
option_feedback: Other costs in the step, such as attention, communication and launches, do not shrink with the weight format, and an expansion pass would add traffic.
Right. Fewer bytes read is what a memory-bound step needs, and the kernel has to read them in the narrow format for that to happen.
Bytes stored are also bytes moved. When reading weights is the limit, moving fewer of them shortens the step.

questions.prompt: DeepSeek’s internal FlashMLA decode kernel is 5–10% faster than the public one, yet end-to-end performance differs by at most 5%. Why?
options: Attention is only one kernel among many in each decode step
The public kernel is used only during prefill
End-to-end measurements round away differences that small
questions.why: A kernel speedup shortens the step only by that kernel’s share of the step’s time. Matrix products, communication and other kernels make up the rest of each decode step and are unchanged.
questions.hint: What share of a step does the faster kernel occupy?
option_feedback: Correct. A 10% faster kernel that takes, say, half the step saves about 5% of the step.
The kernel in question is the decoding kernel, so it runs on every decode step.
The gap is real and follows from the kernel’s share of step time, not from measurement rounding.

transfer: A teammate suggests using a smaller numerical format to speed up your endpoint. What would you want to know before adopting it?
Identifies limiting operation and resource
Checks hardware/kernel support
Tests numerical/task quality and end-to-end latency

I would first find which operation and which resource are taking the time. Storing fewer bytes helps when data movement is the limit, and it does nothing for a scheduling delay or a slow conversion step. I would check that the hardware and kernels support the format, compare outputs with a reference and evaluate task quality. Then I would rerun the same workload to see whether the latency users see actually improves.
LESSONS.takeaway: An operation takes as long as the slowest of moving its data, doing its arithmetic and coordinating its kernels, so speeding up the other costs does not shorten it.

activity.title: Choose which limit to investigate first.
activity.intro: For one toy operation, the amount of arithmetic divided by the arithmetic rate gives 2 milliseconds. Moving the needed data at the available bandwidth gives 8 milliseconds. Assume ideal overlap between the two. This is an estimate for one operation, not a measured whole-model latency.

fields.label: What is the ideal lower bound in milliseconds?
fields.why: With ideal overlap, the lower bound is the larger cost: max(2, 8) = 8 milliseconds.

fields.label: Which limit dominates this estimate?
options: compute
The arithmetic rate
memory
The rate at which data can move
fields.why: The data movement takes longer than the arithmetic under these assumptions. Faster arithmetic alone would leave the 8-millisecond limit.

options: peak
Only the advertised peak arithmetic rate
trace
A runtime trace showing where time and data movement go
name

levels.1:
A GPU is a processor built to perform enormous numbers of arithmetic operations in parallel, which suits language models because they are mostly arithmetic. But the arithmetic units can only work on numbers that have already reached them. Model weights and working state live in memory, and during execution the data has to travel from there to the units doing the calculation, with some results traveling back, and that movement takes time.

So there are two different questions to ask about memory. Capacity is how much data fits, and bandwidth is how many bytes can move per second, and a model can fit comfortably and still run slowly because every step has to move a lot of data. The GPU’s large main memory is usually called HBM, short for high-bandwidth memory, while much smaller and much faster storage sits closer to the arithmetic units. A good deal of an engine developer’s work goes into arranging calculations so the data they need is already close by.

Picture an operation that needs eight milliseconds to fetch its data and one millisecond to do its arithmetic. Doubling the arithmetic speed leaves the eight-millisecond transfer exactly where it was, because data movement sets this operation’s pace. If the engine groups enough work together that the same fetched weights get used many times, each byte moved supports more arithmetic, and the arithmetic units stay busier until some other cost becomes the limit.

The work itself is carried out by kernels, the programs that run individual GPU operations, and many speedups come from better kernels that avoid writing an intermediate result out to slow memory, lay data out more efficiently or merge several small operations into one. Storing each number in fewer bytes helps too. That is one purpose of quantization, which represents values in a more limited format, though it raises its own questions about rounding, model quality and whether the hardware handles the format efficiently. For any optimization, what you want to know is which cost it removes and whether that cost dominates your workload.
levels.2:
Take one matrix product. A batch X[B,d] multiplied by a BF16 weight mapping d to h costs 2Bdh FLOPs and moves about 2(dh + Bd + Bh) bytes, the weight once plus the inputs and outputs. When B is much smaller than d and h the weight term dominates, so the arithmetic intensity, FLOPs per byte moved, comes out at about 2Bdh / 2dh = B. Compare that with the device’s ridge point, its compute rate divided by its bandwidth. NVIDIA’s H100 SXM datasheet lists 989 TFLOP/s of dense BF16 compute and 3.35 TB/s of HBM bandwidth, a ridge near 295 FLOPs per byte, so below roughly 295 tokens per step this product is limited by memory on that device.

That is why decode is cheap per token at moderate batch sizes. A step that must read 8 GB of weights at 3.35 TB/s cannot finish in less than 2.4 ms whether the batch holds one token or two hundred, so within that range a larger batch is almost free per token. Storing weights in FP8 halves the bytes, but FP8 compute is also twice as fast as BF16, so the ridge measured in tokens barely moves. Mixture-of-experts models complicate the count, because each expert sees only the tokens routed to it and so runs at a much smaller batch. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production gives this as a reason to spread decode across 64–128 GPUs. With the experts spread that widely, each GPU holds fewer of them, each expert collects a larger batch, and memory traffic per step falls. DeepInfer targets NVIDIA SM100 (Blackwell) GPUs and Huawei’s Ascend AI chips, whose figures differ from the H100’s, but the reasoning carries over.

Inside a GPU, data moves through a hierarchy of storage, from HBM to a shared L2 cache to the shared memory and registers of each streaming multiprocessor (the GPU’s individual processing cores), each level smaller and faster than the one before. A matrix kernel loads tiles of both operands into shared memory, reuses each tile many times from there and writes only the finished output. DeepInfer’s dense products go through DeepGEMM, DeepSeek’s library of matrix-multiplication kernels (bf16_gemm_nt and FP8 variants in layers/linear.py). Its FP8 path quantizes activations to E4M3 with one power-of-two scale per 32 channels (get_fp8_cast_params), a format that the tensor cores, the GPU’s dedicated matrix units, consume directly.

Kernel fusion, which merges several operations into one kernel, cuts the traffic between them. Run separately, normalization, rotary embedding, a rotation, an FP8 cast and a cache store would each read their input from HBM and write their output back. DeepInfer’s fused_norm_rope_hadamard_cast_store_kvcache in tilelang_ops/fused_transform.py does all five in one kernel and keeps the intermediates on chip, so the FLOP count is unchanged while four round trips through HBM and four kernel launches disappear.

Launch overhead matters most in decode, where each kernel does little work. The CPU spends microseconds enqueueing each launch and a step can contain hundreds, so DeepInfer records the whole sequence once as a CUDA graph and replays it with one call. Graphs are captured for fixed batch sizes in deepinfer/worker/cuda_graph_runner.py, where build_graph_batch_sizes produces 1, 2 and 4 and then every multiple of 8 up to the maximum, and select picks the smallest captured size that fits. Nine tokens therefore run as a 16-row graph with 7 rows (44%) of padding, while fifty-seven run as 64 with 11%. Finer intervals would waste less compute, but each extra graph costs memory and capture time.

The engine also guards the CPU side. execute_main_model in worker/model_runner.py runs inside forbid_cuda_sync(), which raises an error on any blocking CPU–GPU synchronization during launch. A single stray .item(), which copies one GPU value to the CPU, would make the CPU wait for the GPU to drain, and the asynchronous scheduler that overlaps CPU bookkeeping with GPU work would stop overlapping. tests/test_cuda_sync_guards.py enforces the rule.

Quantization saves bytes at some cost in precision, and the format decides how much. Block scaling with 32 elements per scale limits how far one outlier can distort its neighbors. DeepSeek’s Q&A lists MXFP4 (FP4 values with one power-of-two scale per 32) for routed expert weights, and an FP4 format with E4M3 scales per 16 values for the main KV cache. A narrower format shortens a step only where bytes were the limit, and only if a kernel consumes it directly instead of running a separate pass to expand it back to BF16.
levels.3:
The bound used above is the roofline model, which Samuel Williams, Andrew Waterman and David Patterson introduced in 2009. It says a kernel cannot run faster than the compute peak, or than bandwidth times arithmetic intensity, whichever is lower. Reiner Pope and colleagues at Google applied it to transformer inference in 2022, showing how batch size, sequence length and partitioning across chips move each operation between the two limits, and the Scaling Book’s roofline chapter and inference chapter, written by Google DeepMind researchers, give the most direct modern treatment. Both limits are ceilings, and real kernels fall short of them by amounts that depend on how they are written.

How far short is usually reported as model FLOPs utilization, MFU, from Aakanksha Chowdhery and colleagues’ 2022 PaLM paper, which divides the model’s necessary FLOPs per second by the hardware peak. Deciding what counts as necessary takes judgment. DeepInfer’s csrc/engine/flops_estimator.hpp weights each contraction by precision (FP4 as 1, FP8 as 2, BF16 as 4) to express work in FP8-equivalent FLOPs, excludes the draft model’s work, padding and replicated experts, and omits normalizations. Each choice is defensible and each moves the number, so two MFU figures are comparable only under the same conventions.

Measurements have shown how much of a model’s runtime goes to moving data. Andrei Ivanov and colleagues’ “Data Movement Is All You Need” (MLSys 2021) profiled BERT training and found that matrix multiplications accounted for nearly all the FLOPs but a much smaller share of the runtime, with the rest going to memory-bound element-wise operations and normalizations that fusion and better layouts could recover. Tri Dao and colleagues’ FlashAttention (2022) designed attention around that traffic, computing softmax piece by piece so exact attention could be tiled and the full score matrix never reached HBM. Later versions divided the work better and used the asynchronous copy engines and FP8 support of Hopper, NVIDIA’s previous GPU generation, and DeepSeek’s FlashMLA, which DeepInfer calls, adapts the idea to latent attention.

A faster kernel speeds up the whole step only by its share of the step’s time. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production gives an example. The public FlashMLA lacks one hand-tuned assembly optimization that makes DeepSeek’s internal decode kernel 5–10% faster, yet end-to-end performance differs by at most 5%, because attention is one kernel among many in a step. A reported kernel speedup says little about end-to-end speed unless it comes with the kernel’s share of step time at the target batch size and context length. Kan Zhu and colleagues’ NanoFlow (2024) works on the step instead of the kernel, splitting a batch into nano-batches so that compute-bound, memory-bound and network-bound operations overlap on one device, which raises utilization without making any single kernel faster.

How far to push fusion and low precision is still unsettled. At one extreme, “megakernels” fuse a whole forward pass into one persistent kernel to remove launch gaps entirely, and the Q&A says DeepSeek’s Mega MoE fused kernel beats unfused MoE at every expert-parallel and batch size within a scale-up domain, the group of GPUs joined by the fastest links. The price is portability, and DeepInfer maintains separate NVIDIA and Ascend paths. Evidence about low-precision formats holds only for the models tested, and perplexity on generic text often misses damage that shows up on reasoning or long-context tasks, which is why DeepInfer ships task evaluations in eval/ (the AIME math competition, GPQA graduate science questions and the HLE expert-level exam) alongside a perplexity reference in tests/models/offline_decode_ppl.json. A roofline also predicts real performance poorly once communication and scheduling interleave, so these trade-offs still have to be measured on the workloads users actually run.
