LESSONS.title: Batching and overlapping CPU with GPU work
LESSONS.goal: How grouping requests into one model step saves work, and why a grouped request can still wait longer.
LESSONS.recall: Why can reusing the same weights across requests improve arithmetic intensity?
LESSONS.predict: If one request finishes early in a fixed batch, must its slot stay empty?
example: A batch holds a short answer and a long answer, and the short one finishes first. What should the engine do with its place in the batch?
The finished request needs no more model steps. Its state can be released once nothing still reads it, and the long answer keeps its own separate state.
With a fixed batch, the short request’s place stays empty until the whole group finishes. Continuous batching instead admits a waiting request between steps and gives it fresh state of its own.

Reusing the place raises overall throughput. The newcomer still waited before it was admitted, though, and each step still takes time, so per-user delays have to be measured before anyone claims that each user got a faster answer.

questions.prompt: What does continuous batching let the engine do?
options: Share one request’s private history with everyone
Replace completed requests between steps
Skip attention for every request
questions.why: The engine re-forms the active group between steps, so a waiting request can take the place of one that finished.
questions.hint: Which unit finishes on its own schedule?
option_feedback: Batched requests share weights and execution steps, but each keeps its own private history.
Right. The group changes between steps, so a waiting request can fill a finished request’s place.
Every request still needs attention over its own context. Batching only groups the work.

questions.prompt: Before asynchronous scheduling, DeepInfer’s GPU sat idle while the CPU post-processed step N and scheduled step N+1. With that CPU work overlapped with the GPU’s forward pass, what sets the time per decode step?
options: The CPU work plus the GPU work, because overlap leaves every phase in place
The GPU’s forward and sampling work, as long as the CPU work for the next step is shorter
The CPU work alone, because the GPU now runs in the background
questions.why: In steady state the CPU prepares step N+1 and finishes step N−1 while the GPU runs step N, so the two lanes run side by side and the longer one sets the pace. In decode that is usually the GPU.
questions.hint: Once both lanes run at the same time, which one finishes last?
option_feedback: Adding the two is the serial case. Overlap removes the gap where the GPU waited for the CPU.
Right. The CPU work hides inside the GPU work, so the step takes about as long as the GPU’s part.
The GPU still has to run every forward pass, and overlap cannot make that work disappear.

questions.prompt: An async rewrite returns each step's output objects to their pool immediately, deleting the deferred release. What is the main risk?
options: Slightly more code to review
A later step reuses memory that a consumer of the earlier step is still reading
Lower GPU utilization during prefill
questions.why: Under overlap, step N's outputs are still being read while step N+1 runs. Recycling them early lets new data overwrite bytes that still have a reader.
questions.hint: Who still holds a reference to those objects when the next step starts?
option_feedback: The risk is a real lifetime bug, which a style review would not catch.
Right. The deferred release keeps every object out of the pool until all of its readers have finished.
GPU utilization is unaffected. The problem is that a shared buffer can end up holding the wrong data.

transfer: Describe one useful way for CPU work and GPU work to overlap, and one moment when the engine must still wait.
Shows two execution resources
Names the data dependency causing a wait
Includes startup or draining cost

The CPU can prepare independent metadata for a future step while the GPU calculates the current step, so the GPU does not sit idle afterward. The CPU must still wait before it reads results that have not finished, and it cannot release or overwrite buffers that an unfinished operation still uses. Overlap also has a startup cost before the pipeline fills and a draining cost at the end.
LESSONS.takeaway: Batching spreads the cost of each model step across several requests, and the scheduler decides which requests share each step and when they join.

levels.1:
Suppose ten people are using the same model at once. Their questions and histories differ, but every one of their requests runs through the same weights, so an engine can compute part of their work together instead of running each request from start to finish on its own.

That grouping, called batching, pays off because each weight read from memory now serves several requests. Many small matrix operations merge into a few large ones that keep the GPU’s arithmetic units busy, and fixed costs such as launching each GPU operation are spread over more useful work.

The requests still have separate lives, though. One person wants a one-line answer and another wants a long report, and if the engine fixes the group at the start and holds it until everyone is done, the short request’s place sits idle while the long one keeps generating. Continuous batching lets the group change between execution steps instead, so when a request finishes, a waiting one takes its place on the next step with fresh state of its own. The hardware stays busier, and no request ever sees another’s conversation.

Deciding what goes into each step is the job of the scheduler. It has to stay within memory limits while dividing every step among new prompts, long prompts and answers that are already streaming back to users.

The GPU can also sit idle for reasons that have nothing to do with the batch. Most of an engine’s coordination code runs on the CPU, which prepares each step, launches the GPU’s operations and processes what comes back, and if the GPU finishes a step and then waits while the CPU gets the next one ready, its arithmetic capacity goes unused. Engines close that gap by having the CPU prepare the parts of a later step that don’t depend on results still being computed while the GPU works on the current one, which they call asynchronous execution. The 2024 NanoFlow paper pushes the same idea inside the GPU, running compute, memory and network work at the same time so that no single resource waits on another.

None of this promises that any one request gets faster. A bigger batch takes longer per step and a new request may have to wait for a free place, so total tokens per second can rise while a particular user waits longer for the first word of their answer. That is why a scheduler is judged on two measurements, the useful work it completes per second and the waits that individual requests experience.
levels.2:
Batching helps decode most because of what one decode step has to read. Each request in a batch contributes one new position (more under speculative decoding, covered in a later lesson), yet the step reads every active weight from GPU memory once however many requests there are. The time that read takes, roughly the weight bytes divided by memory bandwidth, buys one token when one request is running and sixty-four tokens when sixty-four are. The batch can’t grow for free indefinitely, because the arithmetic grows with it and so does attention, which reads each request’s own KV cache. Once those catch up with the weight read, every extra request makes the step longer.

In DeepInfer the choice of who joins a step is made by a scheduler written in C++ (csrc/engine/scheduler.hpp), which the engine’s per-step function, LLMEngine.step, calls once per step. A request starts in the waiting queue, moves to prompted once its prefill is done and to running while it generates. Two settings bound each step, max_num_seqs on how many requests take part and max_num_batched_tokens on how many positions it computes. When a prompt is too long for the token budget that remains, _schedule_prefill runs only a piece of it now and leaves the rest for later steps, which is chunked prefill, and a helper called _adjust_chunk_size moves the cut so it never lands inside an image’s tokens.

Decode runs into a different limit. Every running request needs room for its next position in KV memory, which a block manager hands out in fixed-size blocks, and when _schedule_decode finds no free block it preempts a running request. Depending on the stop_preempted_request setting, that request either ends with status FINISHED_PREEMPTED or is reset and put back at the front of waiting to be recomputed from scratch. Requests producing structured output always stop, because their grammar state can’t be rebuilt.

In the default engine a step is either all prefill or all decode, and every data-parallel rank has to make the same choice, because all of them join the same expert-parallel communication inside the step (the parallelism lesson explains why). The scheduling function _schedule settles it with a vote, using an all-reduce, a collective operation that combines every rank’s preference. A rank with nothing to do still runs an empty placeholder step so that the group communication lines up.

The CPU’s share of each step is where asynchronous execution comes in. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production breaks decode step N into schedule(N) → forward(N) → sample(N) → post-process(N). Scheduling and post-processing are pure CPU work, and post-processing can’t start until the sampled tokens come back from the GPU, so when the stages run in order the GPU idles through post-process(N) and schedule(N+1). DeepInfer’s zero-overhead scheduling has the CPU schedule step N+1 and finish post-processing step N−1 while the GPU runs step N. A step then lasts as long as the slower of the two lanes, which in decode is normally the GPU’s forward pass and sampling. If the CPU’s work ever grew past the GPU’s, the CPU would set the pace, and that is why the engine’s main Python file, llm_engine.py, carries a TODO to remove per-request Python work from each decode step.

The overlap itself lives in Worker.execute_model_step in deepinfer/worker/worker.py, the function that runs one step on a GPU. It runs the forward pass for the current step, then post-processes the previous step, then samples the current one. For decode steps with DEEPINFER_ZERO_OVERHEAD_SCHEDULING turned on, it saves the current step’s state in prev_step_state so that its post-processing can overlap the next forward pass. Prefill steps are post-processed straight away.

The price is that the CPU schedules step N+1 before it knows what step N produced. When the engine drafts several tokens per step, the CPU doesn’t yet know how many were accepted, and so doesn’t know each sequence’s true length. A function called _correct_seqlens_qk repairs the lengths on the GPU, building a remap from each request in the new batch to its row in the previous one (−1 for newcomers) and adding the previous step’s num_accepted_tokens, so the CPU never has to stop and wait. Object lifetimes need the same care. The docstring of step warns that its outputs are released on the next call unless the caller clones them, and a DeferredRelease class holds each step’s metadata and outputs until the next sampling synchronization point, pre_sampler_sync, so nothing goes back to a pool while someone may still be reading it.
levels.3:
Once continuous batching became standard, the argument moved to how prefill, which is heavy on arithmetic, and decode, which needs little arithmetic but is sensitive to latency, should share hardware. Some systems, Sarathi-Serve among them, cut prompts into chunks and mix them into decode steps so a long prompt never stalls the streams already running. Others put the two phases on different machines, so they stop interfering and each pool can be sized for its own phase. DeepSeek’s production system takes the second route, and DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production describes separate deployments for the vision encoder, prefill and decode. On a prefill machine the chunk size isn’t fixed. A fitted quadratic cost model, cost(q, c), predicts how long a step will take from the number of new tokens q and the length c of the prefix already computed, and the scheduler takes the largest chunk that fits the step’s time budget, up to 32,768 tokens. The open-source engine, when one engine does both jobs, alternates whole prefill and decode steps instead.

The same Q&A credits SGLang and NanoFlow as the prior work its CPU–GPU overlap follows. NanoFlow, from Kan Zhu, Baris Kasikci and colleagues in 2024, goes further than hiding CPU work. It splits a batch into nano-batches inside one GPU so that operations limited by arithmetic, by memory and by network all run at once. Its authors also push against the common assumption that serving is limited by memory, arguing that for most workloads it is limited by arithmetic and that engines lose throughput by running those different kinds of work one after another. They report up to 1.91× the throughput of the systems they compared against and estimate that NanoFlow reaches 50–72% of the best their hardware could deliver, measured on their own models and workloads.

Because a larger batch trades per-user speed for total throughput, scheduling claims are best compared as curves. The DeepInfer repository’s README plots decode output throughput against per-user speed, the tokens per second one user sees, measured on 64 SM100 GPUs, with each point a different number of concurrent requests. Running more requests moves a deployment along that curve toward more throughput and less speed per user, so a single tokens-per-second figure can come from nothing more than a bigger batch. A scheduler change helps only if it moves the whole curve outward, and a report that lets you check that gives time to first token and inter-token latency percentiles at the concurrency you plan to serve, along with how many requests were sampled.

Overlap brings its own class of bugs, in which data still in use is released or overwritten. DeepInfer’s DeferredRelease waits a full step before returning metadata and output objects to their pools, and cloned KV blocks are unpinned only after a CUDA event fires, a marker the GPU reaches once the copy has finished. A copy or a delayed free that looks wasteful may be what stops a later step from overwriting bytes an earlier consumer is still reading, so before deleting one an engineer has to find every reader of that buffer and the event that orders them. Early stops, cancellations, preemption with recompute and mixed sequence lengths all deserve tests, because each changes which request occupies a row between the step that was scheduled and the step that gets post-processed.

Some of this remains unsettled. Output lengths are unknown when a request is admitted, so every preemption policy is a guess about which request will finish soon, and recomputing a preempted request repeats its prefill. Speculative decoding complicates asynchronous scheduling too. In DeepInfer the CPU can fix only the total verification budget for step N+1, because step N’s confidence estimates haven’t come back yet, and a GPU kernel later divides that budget among requests. And the CPU’s work per step grows with the number of active requests, so at very large batches the coordinating CPU can become the bottleneck before the GPU does.

LESSONS.title: KV memory, paging and prefix reuse
LESSONS.goal: How an engine stores each request’s attention state, organizes that memory in blocks, and reuses state computed for an earlier request with the same beginning.
LESSONS.recall: What computation does a KV cache avoid, and what work remains?
LESSONS.predict: If two prompts share the same first 1,000 tokens, can that prefix be reused when their model weights differ?
example: Two requests have the same prompt token IDs. The second uses a different adapter that changes attention. Can it reuse the first request’s keys and values?
The first request’s keys and values came out of its base weights and its adapter. They are numerical results of that particular computation, so the prompt IDs alone do not determine them.

The second adapter can produce different attention state from the same IDs. Reusing the first request’s state would mix values from two different models without raising any error, because the tensors have the same shapes.

The fix is to put the model and adapter identity into the cache key, or to invalidate the affected state when the adapter changes. A test alternates the two adapters and compares cached results against uncached reference runs.

questions.prompt: How do paging and prefix caching relate?
options: They are the same mechanism
Paging manages where state is stored, and prefix caching reuses prefixes already computed
Both compress text
questions.why: They can be combined, but they remove different waste. Paging removes fragmented memory, and prefix caching removes repeated prefill.
questions.hint: One asks where state fits, and the other asks whether it already exists.
option_feedback: They often work together, but one decides where state lives and the other decides whether it already exists.
Right. Paging manages where blocks go, and prefix caching skips recomputing a beginning that was already processed.
Neither one compresses text. Both handle numerical attention state.

questions.prompt: A conventional cache stores one key and one value per KV head, per layer, per token. A model shares 8 KV heads among its 32 query heads (grouped-query attention) instead of giving each query head its own. What does that change?
options: The weights shrink by a factor of four, and the cache stays the same
Each token’s cache entry is a quarter of the size, so about four times as many tokens fit, and decode reads a quarter as many cache bytes
Nothing, because each query head still attends over every position
questions.why: The per-token cache size is proportional to the number of KV heads. Sharing 8 among 32 query heads cuts it to a quarter, which raises how many live tokens fit and lowers the cache traffic each decode step reads.
questions.hint: Which count appears in the cache formula: query heads or KV heads?
option_feedback: Only the key and value projections get smaller, which is a small share of the weights. The large effect is on the cache.
Right. Fewer KV heads means fewer stored vectors per token, which saves both memory and per-step reads.
The queries still attend over every position, but they read shared keys and values, so there is less to store and read.

questions.prompt: A team wants to key the prefix cache on token IDs alone. They argue that two LoRA adapters of the same rank produce tensors of the same shape. Should the change be accepted?
options: Accept, because equal shapes mean the cached values are interchangeable
Reject, because the adapter is an input to the cached keys and values, so it belongs in the key
Accept if hit rate rises after the change
questions.why: Keys and values are numerical results of the weights that computed them. Equal shapes only hide the mismatch.
questions.hint: List every input that determined the cached numbers.
option_feedback: Shape says nothing about values, and two adapters can compute different keys for the same IDs.
Right. The key needs model and adapter identity, and a test should alternate adapters against uncached references.
A higher hit rate would be the symptom of the bug, because wrong state would be found more often.

transfer: A cache finds more matching prefixes, but requests take longer. Give a possible explanation and a measurement that would test it.
Includes transfer or lookup cost
Compares saved computation with added cost
Measures latency, not hit rate alone

Looking up or fetching the saved state may take longer than processing the prefix again. A hit shows that stored work was found, but not that fetching it saved time. I would time lookup, transfer and the remaining prompt computation separately for hits and misses, then compare time to first token on a representative workload. I would also check whether the transfers slow down other requests.
LESSONS.takeaway: A prefix-cache hit saves time only when the stored state was computed by the same model and adapter and can be fetched faster than it could be recomputed.

levels.1:
The KV cache you met in the attention lesson, the keys and values saved from every earlier position of a request, spares the engine from recomputing a request’s whole history at each generation step. Once many requests are served together, that saved state becomes the engine’s main memory problem, because each request’s cache keeps growing until it finishes, and new requests keep arriving that may begin with text the engine has already processed.

Suppose every request were given one contiguous stretch of memory. Nobody knows in advance how long an answer will run, so the engine would have to reserve room for the longest possible answer, and requests finishing at different times would leave holes of awkward sizes between the ones still running. Much of the memory would sit reserved or stranded instead of holding state.

Woosuk Kwon and colleagues fixed this in their 2023 PagedAttention paper, the work behind the vLLM engine, by borrowing paging from operating systems. The state is cut into fixed-size blocks, and each request keeps a table that maps its logical positions to whichever physical blocks happened to be free, much as an operating system maps a program’s virtual pages onto scattered physical memory. A request claims a new block only when its last one fills, and two requests that begin identically can point at the same blocks.

Once blocks can be shared, work can be shared too. If thousands of requests start with the same long system instructions, the engine can keep the keys and values computed for that common beginning, the prefix, and attach them to each new request instead of running the prefix through the model again. Engines call this prefix caching. The SGLang paper keeps saved prefixes in a tree, a design its authors call RadixAttention, so a request that shares only the first part of a beginning can still reuse that part.

Reuse is correct only when the match is exact in a particular sense. The text has to tokenize to the same IDs, and the model that processes those IDs has to perform the same computation, so a request served with a different adapter gets different keys and values from identical prompt text and cannot borrow the first request’s state.

A correct hit can still be a slow one. The saved prefix may live on another machine, and looking it up, transferring it and attaching it to the new request all take time, so for a short prefix recomputing it can be quicker. That is why a hit rate, which counts how often stored work was found, says nothing by itself about whether users waited less.

The memory all this takes grows with the amount of live context, which is the number of requests times their lengths, so in a conventional cache doubling both makes the stored state four times larger. DeepSeek’s models compress that state, as the next lesson explains, which changes the accounting without removing the pressure.
levels.2:
In a conventional cache each layer stores one key vector and one value vector per KV head for every token, so a token costs 2 × layers × KV_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_element bytes, and the whole cache is that times the number of live tokens across all requests. A model shaped like Llama 3 8B, with 32 layers and 8 KV heads of dimension 128 stored in BF16, needs 128 KiB per token, so 32 requests of 8,192 tokens each hold 32 GiB of cache before the engine has set aside any working memory. The number of KV heads is the term designers can change most easily. Llama shares its 8 KV heads among 32 query heads (grouped-query attention), and giving every query head its own would make the cache four times larger and every decode step read four times as many cache bytes.

DeepSeek V4.1 does not fit that formula, and DeepInfer’s cache allocator, deepinfer/worker/cache_engine.py, shows how far it departs. The main cache, ca_cache, has shape [num_blocks, block_size // ratio, 1, bytes_per_token] because several positions are folded together before anything is stored, and each stored entry is a latent vector from which keys and values are derived later. An entry takes 288 bytes in a 4-bit format with one scale per 16 values, or 528 bytes in MXFP8. Beside it sits an indexer cache, ica_cache, holding small 4-bit keys that sparse attention uses to decide which blocks are worth reading at all.

The sliding-window state is handled differently again. A sliding-window layer only looks at the most recent positions, so its memory never grows with context, and DeepInfer keeps it out of the pages entirely. Each request gets one fixed slot in swa_cache sized for window + DEEPINFER_MAX_BACKTRACKING_TOKENS positions, which by default is 128 + 6 = 134 per layer, the extra 6 letting speculative decoding back up after its 5 draft tokens are rejected. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production puts the stored size of that state at about 1.4 MB per sequence. Paged memory therefore grows with context length while slot memory grows with the number of concurrent requests, which is why get_num_state_slots sizes the slot pool from max_num_seqs (1.2 × max_num_seqs + 1).

The pages are handed out by a block manager written in C++, csrc/engine/block_manager.hpp. It keeps free blocks in a doubly linked list, reserves block 0 to mean "no block", and gives every block a reference count. allocate takes a free block and sets its count to 1, pin_block adds a reference when another sequence shares the block, and free puts a block back on the list only once its count reaches zero. Before any allocation, can_allocate_nolock answers OK, LATER when the request should wait for blocks to free up, or NEVER when it needs more blocks than exist and has to be rejected.

Forking a request shows how that sharing plays out. When fork_seq branches a new sequence off a computed prefix, the branch starts with a copy of the parent’s block table, so every full block stays shared. The partly filled last block is the exception, because the branch will write new positions into it and must not overwrite the parent’s, so when the branch is scheduled that block is copied into a fresh one, the pair is recorded in clone_blocks, and the request’s state slot is cloned as well. This is copy-on-write at block granularity, the same trick PagedAttention used to let several samples from one prompt share memory.

In DeepSeek’s production system a prefix hit travels a long path, and every leg costs time. The entrypoint first finds the hit by matching a hash chain over metadata, and because the hit length has to be known before the request is routed, that lookup adds directly to the request’s wait. A separate process then pulls the KV from a storage cluster into host shared memory, and a thread inside the engine copies it into GPU memory layer by layer while the forward pass runs. That last copy uses GPUDirect RDMA because the GPU’s own copy engine did poorly on many small block copies. Recomputing a prefix costs work for every token times every parameter, so for prefixes of thousands of tokens the fetch wins easily, while for a couple of hundred tokens recomputation takes only milliseconds and a fixed lookup and round trip of similar size can cancel the gain.
levels.3:
Kwon and colleagues reported that vLLM’s paging gave 2–4× the throughput of FasterTransformer and Orca at the same latency, with larger gains for longer sequences, larger models and decoding methods that share prefixes, such as beam search and parallel sampling. Earlier systems reserved contiguous space for each request’s maximum length, and when memory capacity is what caps the batch, every block reclaimed from that reservation becomes room for another request. The numbers are the authors’ own, on their workloads, but the mechanism carries over to any engine whose batch is memory-bound.

Where the cached state lives decides how requests should be routed, and here the systems disagree. SGLang keeps prefixes in GPU memory in its radix tree, evicts the least recently used ones first and has its scheduler favour requests whose prefixes are already cached, so it pays to send each request to the machine that holds its prefix. DeepSeek chose the opposite. Its block KV lives on a dedicated storage cluster running 3FS, DeepSeek’s distributed file system, and according to DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production it is protected with 10+2 erasure coding, so a read goes out to 11 storage nodes at once and any 10 replies are enough to rebuild the data. Because any prefill machine can read any prefix, the router can ignore where a prefix was computed and balance on load alone, storage can be scaled separately from the GPUs, and a failed compute node loses no cache. Only the sliding-window state stays behind in the host memory of the machine that produced it.

Keeping state for days pays off only because reuse is long-tailed. DeepSeek expires prefixes after 3 days for agent traffic and 7 days for chatbot traffic, because in chatbot traffic a small amount of KV cache is read very many times, and the team reports that a 3-day lifetime would cost chatbot traffic 0.5–1% of its hit rate. These figures are author-reported, and the cache-management code is tied to DeepSeek’s internal infrastructure and is not in the open release.

DeepSeek’s mixed attention also limits how long a hit can be. The block cache sets the hit length in whole 128-token blocks, but the last block is usable only if the sliding-window state for it survived too, and otherwise the engine backs off one block and recomputes it. The Q&A states the overall cap as at most L − 134 tokens for an input of length L, the 128-token window plus 6 positions of speculative backtracking, and the next lesson explains the layer layout that makes this necessary.

Exact reuse is safe only when every input that shaped the cached numbers matches, which means the weights, adapter, tokenization, position encoding and storage format as well as the token IDs. A shared cache also leaks timing, since a hit returns faster than a miss and one user may infer that another recently sent the same prefix, so whether the cache is shared per user, per organization or globally is a security decision as well as a performance one.

Bugs here come in two kinds that need different tests. In an allocation bug a request gets the wrong blocks, which shows up with lengths just below, at and just above a block boundary, with eviction while a request is still active, and with forks from a partly filled block. In a content bug the right blocks hold the wrong values, which shows up only when cached runs are compared against uncached references, for instance by alternating two adapters over the same prompt IDs. A test that merely confirms the lookup succeeded passes in exactly the case where reuse is wrong, because a wrong hit is still a hit.

LESSONS.title: Compressed attention, sliding windows and replay
LESSONS.goal: What changes when a model compresses its attention state, limits which positions each layer reads, shares state across layers, or rebuilds that state approximately.
LESSONS.recall: Why is the conventional KV formula not universal?
LESSONS.predict: If each layer sees the last 128 tokens, is the entire multi-layer model’s dependence limited to 128 original tokens?
example: An engineer argues that because each layer attends over 128 tokens, replaying the last 128 raw tokens restores a 20-layer model’s state exactly. What is missing from the argument?
Take the first token in the replayed region. In the original run, its deeper representations absorbed information that reached it, layer by layer, from positions before the replay boundary.

A replay that starts at the boundary has no access to that upstream state, so it can compute a different deeper representation. The tensors keep their dimensions, but the information from before the boundary is gone.

Exactness needs its own test, comparing the replayed computation with the full reference on identical continuations, including boundary and long-context cases. If an approximation is acceptable, the tasks you intend to serve also need to be evaluated.

questions.prompt: What do MLA, paging and SWA each concern?
options: All three describe the same memory-allocation technique.
What is stored, how memory is organized, and which positions can be read.
All three change how text is split into tokens.
questions.why: MLA changes what is stored, paging changes how memory is organized and SWA changes which positions a query can read. A smaller cache can come from any of them, and each makes a different promise.
questions.hint: Each term answers a different question.
option_feedback: Only paging is about allocation. MLA changes the representation, and SWA changes visibility.
Right. MLA changes the stored representation, paging organizes memory and SWA limits which positions a query reads.
Tokenization happens before any of these, and all three concern attention state.

questions.prompt: DeepInfer finds a block-cache hit for a long prompt, but the saved sliding-window state for the last hit block is missing. What does its policy do?
options: Treats the whole prefix as a miss and prefills from the start
Backs the hit off by one 128-token block and replays that block to rebuild the window state, reusing the block cache unchanged
Uses the block hit as is and leaves the sliding-window layers empty
questions.why: The hit length is set by the block cache, and the window state decides only whether the last block needs recomputing. Replaying one block costs a fixed amount of work, independent of context length, and rebuilds an approximate window state.
questions.hint: Which cache sets the hit length, and which decides whether the last block is recomputed?
option_feedback: That would throw away a block cache that is still valid, and recompute far more than the missing state needs.
Right. Only the last block is replayed, and the replay rebuilds the window state while the block KV is reused as it was.
The sliding-window layers need their recent keys and values to attend at all, so they cannot simply run without them.

questions.prompt: DeepInfer’s level-2 YoCo check compares log probabilities from two truncation modes and finds that mask and compact modes match. What does this establish?
options: Bounded replay matches the full computation with truncation off
The two truncation implementations agree on the tested trajectories and configuration
Truncation is safe for any fine-tuned model
questions.why: Both compared modes truncate, so the check shows they agree with each other. It never compares truncation with the untruncated reference.
questions.hint: Identify the two things actually compared.
option_feedback: Neither run had truncation off, so the gap from the full computation was never measured.
Right. Agreement holds for those two implementations, under the conditions tested.
Compatibility depends on the model’s layer layout, which this check takes as given.

transfer: Why would you avoid turning on a model-specific cache shortcut for an arbitrary model you fine-tuned?
Names architecture/config dependency
Distinguishes exactness from approximation
Requires reference and task-quality comparison

A shortcut can depend on how one architecture produces and consumes state, and a model I fine-tuned may not share those layer-sharing or attention dependencies. I would first establish compatibility, then find out whether the shortcut promises an exact calculation or accepts an approximation. I would compare it against the appropriate reference, test boundary and long-context cases, and evaluate task quality wherever numerical differences are allowed.
LESSONS.takeaway: A smaller attention cache can come from storing a compressed representation, from limiting which positions each layer reads, or from an approximation, and only the approximation changes the model’s results.

levels.1:
So far the KV cache has meant a key and a value saved for every layer and every position. Nothing forces a model to store exactly that, and designers change both what gets stored and how later layers use it, so a memory shortcut that is correct for one architecture can be wrong for another even when both are called transformers.

One kind of change is to what gets stored. Multi-head latent attention (MLA), introduced in DeepSeek’s V2 paper, caches one compressed latent vector per position, and each layer derives its keys and values from that vector when it needs them. The saving comes from how the model represents attention information, so it is independent of paging, which only decides where allocated blocks sit in memory.

Other designs limit what a query can read directly. With sliding-window attention (SWA), a layer lets each position attend only to a recent stretch of the sequence, say the last 128 positions, which bounds both that layer’s attention work and the state it has to keep. Layers build on one another, though, and a recent position’s representation may already carry information that lower layers pulled in from much older positions. A 128-position window in every layer therefore does not mean the model has forgotten everything more than 128 tokens back.

Some architectures go further and let later layers reuse state that earlier layers produced. In the design Yutao Sun and colleagues called “You Only Cache Once” (YOCO) in 2024, one group of layers builds a single cache that all the remaining layers read. DeepInfer has its own producer and consumer layer paths for the DeepSeek model it serves, and that model’s configuration decides which layers play which role.

A shortcut can also give up exactness to save work. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production describes rebuilding a request’s sliding-window state by replaying only its most recent 128 tokens, with attention confined to that segment. DeepSeek calls the result approximate, because the replay never rebuilds the older state that fed into those tokens in the original run.

That can be a sensible trade as long as someone measures what it does to the tasks being served. Showing that two implementations of the shortcut agree with each other proves something narrower than showing that the shortcut matches the full computation.

When reading this part of DeepInfer, it helps to ask of each code path what it stores, what it reuses and what it recomputes. The answer tells you whether the path promises exact numbers or an approximation, and so which comparison would test it.
levels.2:
Stacked windows reach further than any single one. If every layer lets position i read the previous W positions, information can move W positions per layer, so after k layers position i can depend on tokens up to k × W back. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production applies this to V4.1, whose 20 decoder layers each use a 128-token window, and says that rebuilding their sliding-window state exactly would mean running the last 2,560 tokens through all 20 of them.

DeepInfer’s cache allocator, deepinfer/worker/cache_engine.py, keeps separate memory for each kind of state V4.1 needs. The paged block cache holds compressed latent entries of 528 bytes each in MXFP8, an 8-bit format with shared scales, and _kv_bytes_per_token checks that the latent width plus the width used for rotary position information (RoPE) matches that layout. Beside it sits an indexer cache of small 4-bit keys, which sparse attention uses to decide which blocks to read, and every sequence also gets a fixed state slot holding the sliding-window keys and values for the most recent 134 positions of each windowed layer.

Layer sharing follows the YOCO pattern. In DeepInfer’s YoCo runtime, v4_modules/yoco.py, the flag yoco_enabled is true when the configuration value n_prefill_layer is smaller than the total number of layers, and every layer from n_prefill_layer onward is a consumer. Consumer layers compute their block KV from a shared hidden state captured at the first consumer layer, so prefill only has to push the full prompt through the producer layers. The consumers still need sliding-window state of their own, and rebuilding it is where truncation comes in.

The setting DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_MODE picks how that rebuild runs. With off everything is computed. With mask every query row is kept but the window is narrowed so that keys before the kept suffix are invisible, while compact removes the truncated rows altogether, using yoco_boundary_compact to gather the kept positions and compact_yoco_boundary to rewrite cross-layer metadata that still described the old row layout. The kept suffix, DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS, has to cover the window plus the backtracking allowance for speculative decoding, which is why the documented default is 140 tokens against 128 + 6. Mask and compact compute the same function on different numbers of rows, so they should agree with each other, but both differ from off because both cut the long dependency path described above.

DeepSeek’s Q&A spells out the replay rule. When replaying from position s, the query at position i attends only to keys from max(s, i−127) through i. That makes the cost of a replay constant, whatever the context length or layer count, and it is also why the state it produces is approximate.

The prefix-cache hit policy combines these pieces. The block cache decides how long a hit is, and the sliding-window state decides only whether the last block must be recomputed. For an input of length L the hit can be at most L − 134 tokens, and the block cache returns some L1 below that cap, a multiple of 128. If window state is saved for the stretch from L1 − 128 to L1, the hit is L1. Otherwise the engine backs off one block and replays it. For a 10,000-token prompt the cap is 9,866, so L1 is 9,856. With window state present the engine computes the remaining 144 tokens, and without it the hit falls to 9,728 and the engine computes 272, where the first 128 only rebuild window state and the block KV for them is reused untouched.
levels.3:
Most of the evidence for these shortcuts is about cost. DeepSeek-V2 (2024), the paper that introduced MLA, reported a KV cache 93.3% smaller and up to 5.76 times the maximum generation throughput of DeepSeek’s earlier 67B dense model. Those figures compare two of DeepSeek’s own models, and V4.1’s attention differs in its details from V2’s, so they show what latent compression can buy in general and say little directly about V4.1.

The YOCO paper by Yutao Sun, Li Dong, Furu Wei and colleagues describes a self-decoder that produces one global cache for a cross-decoder to reuse, so that prefill can exit early without changing the output. That exactness holds because the model was trained with the sharing in place. DeepInfer’s bounded replay is a separate step added on top of a YOCO-style model, which shortens the consumer layers’ window rebuild and accepts an approximate result. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production says decoder replay nearly halves total prefill computation, but it gives no task-quality numbers for the approximation, so that claim covers cost only.

The equivalence checks in DeepInfer’s YoCo example README differ in how much they exercise. The level-1 check runs on one device in seconds without loading weights and compares the metadata that mask and compact produce, such as window pivots, visible keys and store slots. The level-2 check needs 8 devices and a compatible V4.1 checkpoint, feeds both modes the same fixed teacher-forcing trajectory, and compares log probabilities and top-K entries one by one, with every other DEEPINFER_* variable held equal. At both levels the comparison is between two implementations of truncation, and neither one runs off. Measuring the approximation itself would mean running off and compact on the same trajectories, reporting the log-probability gap by distance from the replay boundary, and then scoring long-context tasks whose answers depend on text well before that boundary.

These paths also assume a particular model. They depend on n_prefill_layer, on which layers use windows and on which layers share KV, and the equivalence script refuses any checkpoint that fails n_prefill_layer < n_layer. A fine-tune of V4.1 keeps that layout, while a different architecture does not, even when its configuration file looks similar.

It is still open whether a model should be trained with the serving approximation in place, which would make replay exact by construction, as YOCO’s layer sharing is. It is also open how much quality loss a replay scheme may cost and on which tasks, and the sources publish no such measurement for DeepInfer’s replay.

LESSONS.title: MoE, parallelism and the slowest worker
LESSONS.goal: How several GPUs divide a model’s weights and work, what they send each other, and why the slowest one sets the pace for the group.
LESSONS.recall: What is the difference between total parameters and parameters used by one token?
LESSONS.predict: If half the tokens choose experts on one GPU, do equal expert counts guarantee balanced work?
example: DeepSeek decodes across 64 GPUs with expert parallelism. Each MoE layer ends with a combine step that every GPU has to join. What happens when some experts are far more popular than others, and what does DeepSeek do about it?

The combine cannot finish until every GPU has processed the tokens routed to its experts. A GPU holding a popular expert therefore sets the pace, and the others wait. Average load says little here, because the layer takes as long as its busiest GPU.

Which experts are popular shifts with traffic, so DeepSeek’s expert load balancer counts each expert’s tokens. In decode it keeps one spare expert slot per GPU, collects load over 1,000 steps and reassigns experts every 10,000 steps, placing extra copies of hot experts on other GPUs so their tokens can be split.

The balance is still imperfect. DeepSeek reports that for decode the busiest GPU’s MoE load is 1.090 times the mean, and that its load balancing overall reaches roughly 80% of a perfectly balanced offline benchmark. Adding GPUs without changing placement would not shorten a layer whose busiest GPU is the limit.

questions.prompt: Which scheme puts different experts on different GPUs?
options: Expert parallelism
Tensor parallelism
Changing the sampling temperature
questions.why: Expert parallelism assigns ownership of experts to devices and routes each token to the owners of its chosen experts.
questions.hint: Name the object being split.
option_feedback: Right. EP gives each device its own set of experts and sends tokens to them.
Tensor parallelism splits the matrices of one operation across devices, so every device takes part in every token’s operation.
Temperature changes how tokens are sampled and has nothing to do with where weights live.

questions.prompt: One logical expert receives 30% of a layer's tokens. EPLB places a second physical copy of it on another rank. What changes?
options: The model gains a new learned function for the router to choose
That expert's tokens can be split between two copies, while the number of logical experts stays the same
The router now picks from physical experts, so routing decisions change
questions.why: A redundant copy adds capacity for an existing logical expert. The gate still selects among logical experts, and the copy only changes where the work runs.
questions.hint: Separate the function the router chooses from where its weights live.
option_feedback: A copy has identical weights, so it adds no new function.
Right. The logical experts are unchanged, and the physical copies share their demand.
The gate selects logical experts, and the logical-to-physical map decides which copy serves a token.

questions.prompt: An engine promises batch-invariant outputs, and it also moves expert copies between GPUs every few thousand steps. Why can the second feature threaten the first?
options: Moving a copy changes which learned function the router selects
Moving a copy can change the order in which partial results are summed, and floating-point sums in a different order can differ slightly
Moving a copy drops the tokens that were in flight on the old GPU
questions.why: A redundant copy has identical weights, but serving tokens from a different place can change the reduction order, and floating-point addition is not associative. That is why DeepInfer disables one DeepEP reduction mode when batch invariance and expert rearrangement are both on.
questions.hint: The weights are identical. What else about the computation can a move change?
option_feedback: The router still chooses among the same logical experts, and the copy holds the same weights.
Right. Identical weights summed in a different order can give results that differ in the last bits.
Inference does not drop routed tokens, and weight moves happen between steps.

transfer: An expert model gets little faster when you double its GPU count. Suggest two possible causes and how you would investigate them.
Includes routing skew or small expert batches
Includes communication/topology
Names a measurement per hypothesis

The router might send a disproportionate share of tokens to a few experts, so some devices finish early and wait. I would measure token demand and execution time per expert and per device. Communication might also grow more expensive as the group grows, especially across slower links between machines, so I would measure those transfers and inspect where the experts are placed.
LESSONS.takeaway: Adding GPUs speeds up a model only when the work is spread evenly across them and the communication between devices costs less than the time saved.

levels.1:
Once a model is too large or too busy for one GPU, the engine has to decide which device stores which weights and which device does which work, and every choice brings its own traffic between devices. The schemes are named after what they divide. Data parallelism hands different requests to different devices, tensor parallelism splits one large matrix multiplication across several devices, pipeline parallelism gives each device a different run of layers, and context parallelism splits the work on one long sequence.

A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model invites one more kind of split. Its feed-forward layers contain many smaller networks called experts, and a router picks a few of them for each token, so any one token touches only a small share of the weights even though all of them have to be stored somewhere. With expert parallelism (EP), different devices own different experts. Each token is sent to the devices that hold the experts it was routed to, and the results travel back to be combined.

Owning the same number of experts does not mean doing the same amount of work, though. Suppose four devices each hold a quarter of the experts, but the router keeps choosing experts that happen to live on one of them. That device receives far more tokens, and because the layer cannot finish until every device has returned its results, the other three finish early and wait. The whole group runs at the speed of its busiest member.

Engine developers therefore count how many tokens each expert receives and time each device separately. When one expert is popular, the engine can store extra copies of it on other devices so they share its tokens. DeepInfer’s expert containers keep logical experts, the learned functions the router chooses among, separate from physical placements, which include those redundant copies. A copy adds capacity, but it gives the router nothing new to choose.

Copies take memory, and moving them means shipping weights between devices. The links themselves differ too, since a fast connection inside one machine behaves very differently from a slower one between machines. Judging a multi-GPU result means knowing where the weights live and how much data crosses which link, and a device count on its own says neither.
levels.2:
DeepSeek splits its model mostly by experts. Tensor parallelism would have to sum partial results across devices inside every layer, using a collective operation called all-reduce, whereas expert parallelism moves tokens instead. After the router picks experts, a dispatch sends each token’s hidden vector to the ranks that own them, and a combine brings the weighted results back. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production pairs this with data-parallel attention, one data-parallel group per expert-parallel rank, so each rank runs attention only for its own requests and never copies their KV caches elsewhere, and all ranks then meet in the MoE layer. Prefill uses 2 to 8 expert-parallel ranks (EP2–8). Decode uses 64 to 128, which DeepSeek calls Wide-EP, and tensor and context parallelism are not used for now.

Decode goes wide because each decode step carries only one new token per request (a few more with speculative decoding), so experts are short of rows to work on. Take a model with 256 routed experts and 8 chosen per token, the routing shape DeepSeek-V3 used, running 60 sequences per rank. Eight ranks together hold 480 tokens per step, which spreads out to about 15 tokens per expert, and a matrix multiplication with 15 rows spends nearly all its time reading the expert’s weights while the arithmetic units sit idle. At 64 ranks the group holds eight times as many tokens, about 120 per expert, and each rank stores fewer experts, so it reads fewer weight bytes per step. That is what the Q&A means when it says Wide-EP cuts the memory traffic of the expert layers.

In the code, the expert containers in v4_modules/moe.py keep four counts apart. logical is n_routed_experts, the range the gate chooses from, and extra is the number of redundant copies. Their sum, physical, is the number of expert weight sets actually allocated and must divide evenly by ep_size, and local = physical / ep_size is how many of them one rank holds. A helper in the load-balancing package, resolve_num_extra_experts, rounds the extra count up until that division comes out exact. The gate itself, TopKGate, adds a learned correction bias (e_score_correction_bias, with a second one for image tokens) to the routing scores before choosing. That bias is part of the trained model, and it is how DeepSeek steered the router toward balance during training without adding an extra loss term.

The trained bias cannot follow the traffic of the day, so at run time the expert load balancer, ExpertLoadBalancer, counts tokens per physical expert at every step and keeps a logical_to_physical_map that lets a popular expert’s tokens be split among its copies. Every so many steps, the placement policy recomputes where experts go. Its stated objective for each layer is to minimize, summed over recent steps, the largest load on any rank, and it works greedily, taking experts in descending order of load and placing each where it raises that sum least. The new weights are then moved between GPUs over NVLink. DeepSeek’s Q&A gives the production settings. Prefill starts with 4 redundant experts per GPU, collects statistics over 100 steps and reshuffles every 1,000, while decode starts with 1 per GPU, uses a 1,000-step window and reshuffles every 10,000 steps.

DeepSeek reports the result as moe_lb, the slowest rank’s MoE load divided by the mean. The Q&A gives 1.074 for prefill on four expert-parallel and four data-parallel ranks, 1.045 for prefill on two of each, and 1.090 for decode. Because the combine waits for the slowest rank, the decode figure means every MoE layer runs about as long as a rank carrying 9% more than the average share. If MoE time grows in proportion to load, perfect balance could shave somewhat under a tenth off that phase, which bounds how much more effort on placement could buy.

The lockstep reaches beyond the MoE layer. Every data-parallel rank must run the same kind of step, because all of them join the same dispatch and combine, so the scheduler holds a vote on whether the next step is prefill or decode, and a rank with nothing to do runs an empty placeholder step instead of skipping ahead.
levels.3:
The evidence for Wide-EP comes from DeepSeek itself. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production shows an EP8-versus-EP64 decode chart produced with the repository’s offline benchmark script, and it says production load balancing reaches roughly 80% of a perfectly balanced offline benchmark. Nobody has reproduced these figures independently, and they come from one model on one hardware generation, with the published benchmarks run on SM100 GPUs inside one scale-up domain. The 80% is DeepSeek’s estimate of what imbalance and routing cost on its own traffic, and another model or traffic mix could land somewhere else.

A wide group also fails as a unit. DeepSeek’s Q&A explains that all the GPUs of an instance form one communication domain, so a single failed GPU makes the whole instance unusable, and on restart the platform sets the EP size to however many healthy GPUs it actually gets. Restarts take minutes, so DeepSeek relies on spare instances and on rerouting requests rather than on fast recovery. Long requests pin a large group in place as well, which is why a decode engine that receives a shutdown notice gets one minute to finish before its unfinished requests and their KV caches are forwarded to other engines. Because the recommended decode setup is EP64 or wider, the smallest efficient deployment is around 64 prefill GPUs plus 64 decode GPUs, and wide expert parallelism only pays for an operator who can run that much hardware.

Moving experts can change numbers as well as speed. The file parallel_utils/userbuffer.py configures DeepEP, DeepSeek’s library for expert dispatch and combine, and it turns off DeepEP’s multiple-reduction mode when batch invariance is enabled together with periodic expert rearrangement. When a copy moves, the order in which partial results are summed can change, and floating-point sums in a different order can differ in the last bits, so an engine that promises the same output regardless of batch has to account for its own load balancer.

Where the devices sit matters more than how many there are. DeepSeek’s Q&A says its fused Mega MoE kernel is the general choice within a scale-up domain at any EP or batch size. Once a group crosses machines, dispatch and combine travel over slower RDMA links, and their traffic grows with the number of tokens times the experts chosen per token times the hidden size. Checking a scaling chart therefore comes down to knowing where the experts live, how many bytes cross which links per step, and which collective waits for whom.

Several problems stay open. Placement is computed from the last 100 to 1,000 steps of load, so it lags behind shifts in traffic, and reacting faster costs more weight shuffling. Speculative decoding multiplies the tokens per step and changes how they route. Image and text tokens route differently, which is why the gate carries two biases, so a mixed workload can be unbalanced in ways neither kind of traffic shows on its own. And a balance figure built on averages can hide the occasional step where one rank stalls all the others.

LESSONS.title: Speculative decoding and DSpark
LESSONS.goal: How a cheap drafter proposes several tokens for the main model to check in one pass, saving time while the main model still decides the output.
LESSONS.recall: What prevents ordinary autoregressive generation from predicting many unknown steps independently?
LESSONS.predict: If draft length doubles, must accepted tokens per second double?
example: In DeepSeek’s production service the draft model proposes 5 tokens per request at every decode step. Should the target model verify all 5?

A draft token becomes part of the answer only if every token before it in the draft was accepted. Its chance of being kept is therefore the product of the acceptance chances up to that point, so the fourth or fifth position of an uncertain draft rarely survives, yet checking it costs as much as checking the first.

DSpark adds a confidence head that predicts how likely each draft token is to be accepted. The scheduler ranks draft tokens by expected acceptance and, using a profile of how the hardware’s throughput changes with verification work, verifies the prefix of each draft that gives the most useful tokens per second.

DeepSeek’s Q&A reports that this cuts the drafts verified per step from 5.00 to between 3.2 and 4.4, while the average accepted length barely moves, from 3.29 to 3.20. The estimated throughput change depends on load: −1.5% at 16 sequences per GPU, +5.4% at 60 and +11.0% at 96. These figures are estimates computed from benchmark data and were not measured in a live A/B test.

questions.prompt: Why verify a draft with the target model?
options: To preserve the target’s intended generation behavior
To avoid loading target weights forever
To train the tokenizer
questions.why: Drafts are proposals, and the target remains the reference for what the output should be.
questions.hint: Who decides what output is acceptable?
option_feedback: Right. Verification keeps the output faithful to the target model.
The target’s weights are used in every verification pass, so speculation never retires them.
Speculation happens at inference time and leaves the tokenizer unchanged.

questions.prompt: Under exact speculative sampling, the drafter proposes token a more often than the target model would choose it. What does verification do with a drafted a?
options: Always accepts it, because the target model checked the position
Accepts it only part of the time, so that a appears in the output exactly as often as the target alone would produce it
Always rejects it and samples a different token
questions.why: The acceptance rule keeps a drafted token with probability min(1, p/q), where p is the target’s probability and q the drafter’s. When the drafter overproposes a token, some proposals are rejected and replaced from a residual distribution, so the output follows the target exactly.
questions.hint: What would happen to a’s frequency in the output if every proposal were kept?
option_feedback: Keeping every proposal would make a appear as often as the drafter likes it, which is more often than the target does.
Right. Partial acceptance trims the drafter’s excess, and resampling on rejection fills in the tokens the drafter underproposes.
Rejecting a every time would make it appear less often than the target intends. The rule only trims the excess.

questions.prompt: DeepSeek’s Q&A estimates that varying the verification length per request changes throughput by −1.5% at 16 sequences per rank and by +11.0% at 96. What best explains the pattern?
options: The confidence head is less accurate when few requests are active
At low concurrency a decode step is memory-bound, so extra verified positions are nearly free. At high concurrency each one costs compute that other requests could use.
Dynamic verification changes the output distribution more at high concurrency
questions.why: Trimming verification saves time only when the verification work has a cost. At low load, verification rides on the weight reads that the step pays for anyway.
questions.hint: When does verifying one more position actually cost time?
option_feedback: The table shows accepted length barely changing at any concurrency, so calibration does not explain it.
Right. The value of trimming depends on whether the step is memory-bound or compute-bound.
Exact verification preserves the target distribution at any length. What changes is throughput.

transfer: Explain how longer drafts could help one user receive tokens faster but reduce the amount of useful work the server does for everyone.
Names saved serial rounds
Names added low-value verification work
Includes concurrency or capacity constraint

A single user may advance through several accepted tokens in one target-model round, which cuts the number of serial waits. Later draft positions have to survive every earlier position, though, so some of the extra checking has little chance of helping. With many requests active, that verification consumes capacity that could serve other users. I would measure accepted progress, drafting and checking time, and latency at the intended concurrency before settling on a draft length.
LESSONS.takeaway: Speculative decoding speeds up generation when the tokens the target accepts are worth more than the time spent drafting and verifying them.

levels.1:
In ordinary generation the model has to pick the next token before it has the input for the prediction after that, so every token costs one full run of the model and the runs happen strictly one after another. For a single person waiting on an answer, the length of that chain of runs is what sets the speed.

Speculative decoding, which Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman and Yossi Matias described in a 2022 paper, gets more out of each run of the main model, which in this setting is called the target. A much cheaper drafter guesses several tokens ahead, and the target then scores all of the guessed positions in one pass, which costs little more than scoring one because the expensive part of a decode step is reading the weights.

The target keeps the guesses it agrees with and corrects the first one it rejects. Leviathan and colleagues gave an acceptance rule, usually called exact speculative sampling, under which the text that comes out follows the same probability distribution the target would have produced on its own. That is a statement about distributions, so two implementations given the same seed can still print different strings and both be correct.

Because a guessed token only counts if every guess before it was kept, the later positions in a draft are worth less than the early ones. If the drafter proposes three tokens, the third one helps only when the first two also survived, yet the target spends the same work checking it.

So the draft length is a bet. A long draft gives a request the chance to move several tokens in one round, but its tail is unlikely to survive, and when many users share the GPU the work spent checking that tail could have gone to someone else. DeepSeek’s DSpark paper makes the bet deliberately. It estimates how likely each prefix of a draft is to survive and weighs that against a measured profile of how its hardware’s throughput changes as verification work grows, and DeepInfer contains the scheduling path that turns those estimates into a verification length for each request.

When you evaluate speculation on your own model, the useful number is accepted tokens per target round set against the time spent drafting and checking, measured at the load you expect. A high acceptance rate on its own does not show a speedup, and a draft length that helps a lone user can waste capacity once the server is busy.
levels.2:
The cost of a long draft follows from how survival compounds. If each position survives with probability 0.8 given that the ones before it did, the second position survives 64% of the time and the fifth only about 33%, but the target pays the same to check the fifth as the first. On top of the accepted drafts the target always contributes one token of its own, either the correction at the first rejection or a bonus token after a draft that survives whole, so every round moves a request forward by at least one token.

What keeps the output faithful to the target is the acceptance rule. A drafted token x, which the drafter proposed with probability q(x), is kept with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), where p(x) is the target’s probability for it. Tokens the drafter proposes less often than the target would are always kept, and tokens it over-proposes are kept only often enough to bring them down to the target’s rate. When a draft token is rejected, the replacement is sampled from what is left of the target’s distribution after removing what the drafter already covered, max(0, p − q) renormalized, which fills in exactly the tokens the drafter under-proposed. Greedy verification, where a draft token is kept only if it is the target’s top choice, is the same rule applied to a target that puts all its probability on one token.

In DeepInfer this happens in Sampler._verification, in the sampler. Each row of logits is first mapped to its request and its position in the draft, and structured-output masks, which block tokens a required format forbids, are applied at every draft position. The sampler then compares the target’s log probability for each draft token with the drafter’s, which was saved during the previous round in a buffer called the MTP info pool, finds each request’s accepted prefix and packs the accepted and newly sampled tokens. After sampling, the draft head (DFlash in this code) runs on the new token to propose the next round’s drafts along with a confidence for each. A note in the sampler points out that this round’s verification reads what the previous round’s draft pass wrote to the pool, and that only the order of work on a single GPU stream keeps that read safe.

How many positions each request gets to verify is decided by the confidence scheduler. On the CPU, MtpVarlen::schedule collects every request’s survival estimates, sorts them from most to least likely, and adds them one at a time on top of the one token every request verifies anyway. At each total size it predicts the step time from a profile measured on the hardware for that graph size, and it keeps the size that gives the most expected tokens per millisecond. If request A’s estimates are 0.9, 0.8 and 0.6 and request B’s are 0.5, 0.2 and 0.1, three extra slots all go to A, and B verifies only its mandatory token. Under asynchronous scheduling the CPU plans step N+1 before step N’s confidences have come back, so it fixes only the total budget, and a GPU kernel in the confidence scheduler recomputes the survival products from the latest confidences and splits that budget among requests.
levels.3:
Leviathan and colleagues showed a 2–3× speedup on T5-XXL with identical outputs, using a small separate model as the drafter. DSpark, from Xin Cheng, Wenfeng Liang and colleagues at DeepSeek, changes both halves of the scheme. Parallel drafters that propose a whole block in one pass lose acceptance quickly toward the end of the block because each guess ignores the others, so DSpark adds a light sequential module that lets later draft tokens depend on earlier ones. It then schedules verification by confidence. The authors report that inside the DeepSeek-V4 serving system it speeds up per-user generation by 60 to 85 percent at matched throughput compared with their earlier production setup, which drafted a single token (MTP-1). The drafter, the traffic and the hardware are all DeepSeek’s own, so the figure describes their system against its predecessor.

DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production separates out the scheduling half. Compared with always verifying all 5 drafted tokens, dynamic lengths verify between 3.24 and 4.44 per step while the average accepted length hardly changes, 3.29 against 3.20. The estimated throughput gain grows with load, from −1.5% at 16 sequences per rank to +5.4% at 60, which is near the production operating point, and +11.0% at 96. That pattern is what the roofline picture from the GPU lesson predicts. With few requests, a decode step is limited by reading weights from memory, so the extra verified positions ride along almost for free and trimming them only throws away accepted tokens, while with many requests each verified position takes compute that another request could have used. The Q&A says these figures were computed from EP64/DP64 benchmark data, so they come from a throughput model and not from a live A/B test.

The scheme only works as well as its confidence estimates. An overconfident head sends verification to tokens that will be rejected, which is why the verification path returns a batch_confidence_error that can be watched in production. The guarantee about the output distribution also holds only if draft and target probabilities are processed the same way at every position, with the same temperature, the same top-k or top-p cut and the same grammar mask, and a stop token that appears inside a draft has to end the sequence there. Speculation also gets in the way of determinism. The repository README asks you to turn variable-length verification off for deterministic sampling. It doesn’t give the reason, but a likely one is that the verification budget is shared across the batch, so how far one request gets verified depends on which other requests happen to be in the batch with it.

Several questions are still open. Nobody has a settled way to keep confidence estimates calibrated as traffic shifts between, say, code and prose, which are drafted with very different success. A drafter trained against a base model may be accepted less often once the target is fine-tuned, and draft length and batch size compete for the same step budget, so tuning one without the other can leave throughput on the table. A report on a speculative setup is most useful when it gives accepted tokens per round, drafting and verification time, inter-token latency percentiles and total throughput at the concurrency that will actually be served, broken down by kind of task.
