LESSONS.title: Correctness, determinism and structured output
LESSONS.goal: What different correctness claims about an engine change mean, and which comparison tests each one.
LESSONS.recall: How does equal output distribution differ from identical outputs?
LESSONS.predict: If JSON parses successfully, have you proved the answer’s facts are true?
example: A cache change produces valid JSON, but its next-token scores disagree with the reference at a page boundary. Should an exactness claim be accepted?
Valid JSON shows that the output followed a structural constraint. It says nothing about whether attention read the right positions or the right cached values.

The disagreement on identical prefixes contradicts the claimed numerical equivalence. The next step is to find the first position and layer where the values differ, starting near the page boundary where the error shows up.

The exactness claim should wait until that mismatch is fixed. If an approximation is acceptable instead, that is a different claim, and it needs a test of real task quality. Valid formatting is evidence for neither.

questions.prompt: What does a JSON grammar guarantee?
options: That every field is true
That the output conforms to the structural constraints it supports
That no sampling occurs
questions.why: Structure and truth are different properties. A grammar constrains form and cannot check facts.
questions.hint: A perfectly formatted wrong answer is still possible.
option_feedback: A grammar constrains form, so a perfectly formatted field can still be false.
Right. The grammar guarantees that the output fits the structure it encodes.
Constrained decoding still samples. The grammar only masks out illegal tokens.

questions.prompt: Does a fixed random seed by itself guarantee batch invariance?
options: Yes
No, because numerical execution and the assignment of random draws also matter
Only for long prompts
questions.why: Different batching can change the order of reductions or which random draw goes to which request, unless both are controlled.
questions.hint: What happens to the numbers before the random selection?
option_feedback: A seed fixes the random draws, but batching can change the numbers those draws act on.
Right. Batch composition can change reduction order and the assignment of random draws.
Prompt length plays no special role, and batch effects can appear at any length.

transfer: Pick an engine change and describe what you would compare to decide whether it is correct. Say what the comparison would and would not establish.
Names a reference
States equality/tolerance/quality criterion
States tested configurations and boundaries

For a cache-read change, I would feed identical token prefixes to the full reference calculation and to the cached path, then compare the next-token scores within a stated tolerance. I would include cache boundaries and interleaved requests. That tests the numerical property directly under those conditions. It does not cover every possible configuration, and it says nothing about whether the model’s answers are factually correct, so those claims need their own checks.
LESSONS.takeaway: Exact numbers, an exact output distribution, a valid format and an acceptable approximation are different correctness claims, and each needs its own reference and comparison rule.

activity.title: Check the numbers before judging a fluent answer.
activity.intro: Two paths receive the same fixed input IDs [1, 4]. The reference returns next-token scores [0.2, 0.8, -0.1]. A changed path returns [0.2, 0.805, -0.1]. Your stated rule permits an absolute difference of at most 0.001 in every score. Both paths still choose the second token when selecting the highest score.

fields.label: What is the largest absolute score difference?
fields.why: The second entry differs by 0.805 − 0.8 = 0.005. The other entries match.

fields.label: Does the changed path pass the stated numerical rule?
options: yes
Yes, because it chooses the same token
no
No, because one score difference exceeds the tolerance
fields.why: 0.005 is greater than 0.001. Matching the highest-scoring token does not establish that the numerical comparison passed.

activity.conclusion: A useful correctness check needs fixed inputs, a reference, a comparison rule and a boundary. Passing this one numerical case would still leave request isolation, stop behavior and task quality unchecked.

levels.1:
Suppose you change how a model reads its cache, and afterwards the program runs, the response sounds fluent and its JSON parses. None of that tells you whether the change preserved the model’s calculation, because an array can have the right dimensions and hold the wrong numbers, and a paragraph can read well while differing from what the reference model would have written.

Format is a good example of a property that is easy to confuse with correctness. Many applications ask for JSON, a text format that programs parse into named fields and values, and an engine can enforce it by giving the sampler a grammar that rules out any continuation the format forbids. The grammar guarantees that the answer parses. It has no way of knowing whether the date in a field is right or whether a fact was invented.

So testing a change starts with naming what it is supposed to preserve. A rewrite of the attention code that claims to be exact should reproduce a trusted implementation’s numbers within a stated rounding tolerance. A new sampling method that claims to be exact should leave the probability of each possible output unchanged, even if individual runs differ. A deliberate approximation is allowed to change the numbers, provided answer quality on real tasks stays within a limit agreed in advance.

Each of those comparisons needs a reference, usually a simpler implementation you already trust, and a rule for deciding whether the new path agrees with it. People sometimes call that check an oracle, though the name promises more than it delivers, since the check only knows about the property it compares.

The inputs also have to be held fixed. If two generators pick different tokens at some step, everything they see afterwards differs, and later disagreements tell you nothing. The usual remedy, called teacher forcing, feeds both implementations the same known continuation and compares their predictions position by position, so the first place where they disagree stands out and nothing after it is muddied by diverging histories.

Many bugs never show up in a pleasant example conversation. A cache bug may appear only when a sequence crosses a block boundary, a state leak may need two requests interleaved in a particular order, and a sampling bug may need a stop token to be proposed in the middle of a draft. Finding them takes test cases built to reach those situations.

Repeatability is its own question. A random seed fixes the draws a sampler makes, but a request can still come out differently when it shares a batch with other requests, because the grouping can change how the arithmetic is done. Keeping a request’s output the same whatever it is batched with is a separate promise, called batch invariance, and a seed does not provide it.

When you report a result, say which of these properties the evidence covers. A comparison of numbers on fixed inputs, for instance, says nothing about task quality or factual accuracy.
levels.2:
Most cases of the same input giving a different output trace back to floating-point addition, which gives different answers depending on the order you add things in. In FP32 the representable numbers near 10⁸ are 8 apart, so adding 1 to 10⁸ and then subtracting 10⁸ gives 0, while subtracting first and then adding 1 gives 1. A matrix multiplication or attention kernel sums thousands of products, and if a larger batch leads it to split that sum into different tiles, the last bits of the result change. Under greedy selection that is enough to swap two nearly tied tokens, and from then on the whole continuation follows a different history.

DeepInfer keeps batch invariance and deterministic sampling as separate settings. Setting DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1, which works on NVIDIA GPUs only, makes a request’s numbers independent of whatever else is in its batch. The runtime configuration file, worker/runtime_config.py, uses the flag to switch the kernel libraries DeepGEMM and TileKernels to deterministic algorithms and to tell the attention backend to do the same, and userbuffer.py turns off a multi-reduction mode in DeepEP, the expert-communication library, while experts are being rearranged. Deterministic sampling needs more on top of that, namely a fixed seq_seed in the request’s SamplingParams and the confidence scheduler turned off, since that scheduler varies how many draft tokens each request verifies. The seed fixes the random draws and batch invariance fixes the numbers those draws act on, so you need both to get the same output twice.

Teacher forcing is built into the sampler through a field called golden_output. Wherever an entry is not −1, the sampler emits that token instead of its own choice, which lets two implementations run over one fixed trajectory. DeepInfer’s YoCo equivalence check uses it to compare log probabilities and the top-K candidates at every position between two ways of truncating the prefill. The same page describes a cheaper first check that runs in seconds on one device without loading weights and compares only metadata, such as which keys each position can see and where they are stored. When the full comparison fails, the most useful thing it can report is the first position, and then the first layer, where the outputs part by more than the tolerance, because errors that begin at a cache-block boundary or at the replay boundary point to particular code.

Structured output runs through the same sampler. According to DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production, each schema is compiled ahead of time on a dedicated machine into a grammar automaton, a state machine that tracks which text may legally come next, and the request picks up the compiled result before it enters the engine. During generation, Sampler._get_so_mask advances each constrained request’s matcher by the tokens accepted in the previous step and fills a bitmask over the vocabulary for the next position. When the engine is drafting several tokens at once, it also walks the matcher through each draft token, building a mask for every draft position until the grammar rejects one, and then calls matcher.rollback so that the grammar state again matches only the text that was committed. The masks are copied on a separate CUDA stream while the model computes its scores, and sampling waits for the copy to finish before applying them.

Failures in this path are kept to the request that caused them. If a matcher throws, the sampler marks only that request as FINISHED_SO_FAILED, because raising the error on the shared sampling path would take down every request in the step. A structured-output request that gets preempted for memory is stopped instead of being recomputed, since its grammar state cannot be replayed.

Each kind of change therefore comes with its own test. Turning on batch invariance should give bit-for-bit equal outputs across batch compositions. An exact kernel rewrite should match the reference elementwise, within a stated tolerance, along teacher-forced trajectories. A speculative sampler can legitimately produce different samples, so it needs a statistical test that its output distribution matches the target model’s. A grammar change needs every output checked by an independent parser, plus a deliberate search for tokens the mask wrongly allowed or blocked, especially tokens whose text straddles a boundary in the grammar.

LESSONS.title: From a fast engine to a usable service
LESSONS.goal: How queues, routing, state transfer and failure handling turn an engine into a service, and when running prefill and decode on separate machines is worth the handoff it creates.
LESSONS.recall: Which parts of an online service live outside the engine loop?
LESSONS.predict: Can putting prefill and decode on separate workers make a small workload slower?
example: DeepSeek keeps prompt caches for days on a dedicated storage cluster, so a returning conversation can skip most of its prefill. What does a hit cost on the way to the GPU, and which parts of that cost does the request actually wait for?

Before the request is routed, the entry point matches its prompt against the cache by walking a chain of hashes over token blocks. The hit length decides which machine gets the request, so this lookup cannot overlap with anything, and every request waits for it.

The matched cache blocks are then fetched from the storage cluster into host memory by a separate process, asynchronously. Copying them into GPU memory happens layer by layer while the forward pass runs, using network cards that write straight into memory so the copy takes no GPU compute.

DeepSeek put the cache on a shared storage cluster instead of each machine’s local memory, so any prefill machine can hit any prefix. Routing can then follow load alone, without sending requests to whichever machine happens to hold their prefix.

A hit still has to be judged by the time users see. If the fetch could not overlap with computation, a slow transfer could make a hit finish later than recomputing the prefix would. Reporting time to first token beside the hit rate shows which case the service is in.

questions.prompt: Putting prefill and decode on different workers creates a need to…
options: Move compatible attention state from the prefill worker to the decode worker
Tokenize the prompt again on the decode worker so it can rebuild the context
Run a separately trained model on each worker
questions.why: Decode continues from the attention state that prefill computed, so that state has to reach the decode worker intact and in a format it can use.
questions.hint: What did prefill produce that decode consumes?
option_feedback: Right. The decode worker needs the keys and values prefill computed, and they have to arrive complete and in a format it can use.
Token IDs alone would force the decode worker to redo the prefill that the split was meant to move elsewhere.
Both stages run the same model with the same weights. Disaggregation only changes which machine does each stage.

questions.prompt: DeepInfer’s scheduler refuses to start a decode-only (COMPLETION) engine unless preempted requests are stopped. Why?
options: Decode-only engines run one request at a time, so preemption would leave them idle
Stopping preempted requests keeps the sampling seed from changing between attempts
A decode-only engine has no prefill path, so it cannot rebuild an evicted request’s cache by recomputing it
questions.why: Recomputing a preempted request means prefilling its prompt and generated tokens again. A decode-only worker has no prefill channel, so the only local options are to stop the request or to send it back through a prefill worker.
questions.hint: What does the recompute branch of _preempt put the request through again?
option_feedback: Decode engines batch many requests, up to max_num_seqs, and preemption exists precisely because several compete for cache blocks.
Seeds play no part in this check. It concerns whether the engine can rebuild cache state at all.
Right. Recomputing is a prefill, and a COMPLETION engine has no prefill channel to run it.

questions.prompt: Your team serves a few requests per second on eight GPUs and is considering splitting prefill and decode. Which evidence would best settle the decision?
options: Goodput under your latency targets on your traffic, comparing the split against a colocated engine with chunked prefill
DeepSeek’s reported tokens per day and revenue per GPU-hour, scaled down to eight GPUs
Peak throughput of the split system at its largest batch size, against a colocated engine serving one request at a time
questions.why: Disaggregation trades handoff cost for less interference between prefill and decode. Goodput on your own traffic, measured against the strongest colocated alternative, shows how that trade works out where you will operate.
questions.hint: Which comparison holds the workload and the strength of the alternative fixed?
option_feedback: Right. Goodput counts only requests that meet both latency targets, and chunked prefill is the colocated design that already reduces the same interference.
Those figures are author-reported at a scale whose smallest efficient unit is 128 GPUs, and they do not scale down linearly.
Comparing a tuned peak against a deliberately weak baseline inflates the gain and ignores the latency targets entirely.

transfer: Describe a simple service for your fine-tuned model. Where does unfinished work live, and what should happen when a user cancels?
Identifies request queue and KV ownership
Includes model/tokenizer/adapter identity
Names cancellation/timeout handling

Requests first wait in a bounded queue and then run in a compatible engine. Each active request owns its working state, including its attention cache. The service records which base model, adapter and input format are in use. When a request completes or is cancelled, the service releases its slot and state once no consumer still needs them. I would get this simple path working before adding remote transfers or separately scaled stages.
LESSONS.takeaway: A service surrounds the engine with admission, cancellation, routing and recovery, and splitting prefill from decode pays only when less interference between them outweighs the cost of moving attention state between machines.

levels.1:
A request spends only part of its life on the GPU.

When a user types a question, a good deal happens before any model calculation starts. A server receives the request, checks that the user is allowed to send it, turns the text into tokens, picks a worker, and may hold the request until a slot frees up. When the model is done, the token IDs are turned back into text and streamed to the user. Each of those steps can add delay, and each can fail.

The program that runs the model calculation is the engine, and a service is the engine plus all of this machinery around it. Keeping the two apart helps when you read a production architecture diagram, and it explains how an open-source engine can be fast and still not be something you could put in front of users. The DeepInfer README, the front page of the public repository, says plainly which parts of DeepSeek’s internal service the release includes and which it leaves out.

Large deployments can give each stage its own workers.

Generating an answer has two phases. During prefill the model reads the whole prompt in one pass, and during decode it extends the answer one token at a time. Because the two load the hardware so differently, a large deployment can run them on separate machines with separate scheduling, an arrangement called disaggregation.

DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production describes a system that goes one step further and gives multimodal encoding, the work of turning images into something the model can read, a pool of its own. The stages still depend on one another, since decode cannot begin until it holds the numerical state that prefill produced.

Every split creates a handoff.

If one machine processes the prompt and another continues the answer, the attention state has to travel between them. That transfer uses network bandwidth, makes the request depend on a second machine, and adds another place where something can go wrong.

For a large or uneven workload, being able to scale prompt work and answer work independently can repay those costs, while a small workload may do better with both stages on one machine. Which case you are in is something only measurements on your own traffic can tell you.

Queues hold work without adding capacity.

When requests arrive faster than the engine finishes them, the unfinished ones pile up, and if the queue may grow without limit, requests at the back wait longer and longer. So a service needs a policy for how much work to admit, how long a request may wait, and what happens when either limit is reached.

Requests also end early, because a user closes the tab or a timeout fires. The service has to notice and release that request’s memory and scheduler slot, or abandoned work goes on occupying space that live requests need.

A first service can be simple.

For a first service around your fine-tuned model, one compatible engine and a test workload that resembles your real traffic are enough. Once it loads the model you intended and behaves as expected, finding out which step of the request’s journey is slow will teach you more than copying an architecture built for a far larger load.
levels.2:
How DeepInfer’s scheduler admits and evicts requests.

Inside the engine, the decision about which requests run at each step belongs to the scheduler. In DeepInfer it is written in C++ (csrc/engine/scheduler.hpp) and called from Python by LLMEngine.step, the function that runs one engine iteration. Two limits govern admission: max_num_seqs, the number of requests that may run at once, and max_num_batched_tokens, the number of tokens one step may process. The offline example script sets them to 4 and 32,768, and a waiting request is admitted only while both leave room.

Once admitted, every running request needs cache space for its next tokens, which the block manager hands out in fixed-size blocks. When no block is free, the scheduler’s _preempt function evicts a request, which is called preemption. What happens next depends on a setting. With stop_preempted_request on, the evicted request simply ends with status FINISHED_PREEMPTED. Otherwise reset_for_recompute clears its cache bookkeeping and puts it back at the front of the waiting queue, so its prompt and generated tokens are prefilled again later. Requests under a structured-output grammar, which forces the output to match a format such as a JSON schema, are always stopped, because the grammar’s progress cannot be rebuilt that way. The offline LLM wrapper defaults to recomputing.

Cancellation is an explicit call.

Ending a request on purpose goes through LLMEngine.abort_request, which hands the request IDs to the scheduler’s abort_sequence. That function scans both the running and waiting queues and marks the matches FINISHED_ABORTED, and on its next pass the scheduler frees their blocks and slots and returns any image buffers to their shared pool. Nothing calls this for you, though. The engine’s docstring says the release has no online-serving wrapper, meaning no server that accepts user connections, so whatever server you put in front of it has to notice a closed connection or an expired deadline and make the call, or the abandoned request keeps generating.

The hooks for disaggregation exist but are empty.

DeepInfer already names the roles an engine could take in a split deployment. The file deepinfer/engine/engine_type.py lists NORMAL, which runs prompts and completions, PROMPT, which runs only prefill, and COMPLETION, which runs only decode. LLMEngine also has hook methods such as init_pd_split, send_processed_prompts and pe_do_save_kvcache, but their bodies are empty in this release. That fits the README, which lists prefill/decode disaggregation as missing while saying most of the engine functionality it needs is present.

One check in the scheduler’s constructor shows what the split costs. A COMPLETION engine refuses to start unless stop_preempted_request is true, because recomputing an evicted request means prefilling it, and a decode-only engine has no prefill path. Recovery from preemption therefore has to go back through a prefill worker, or the request fails.

What the handoff costs.

For the network between machines, DeepSeek’s production Q&A budgets about 400 Gbps for every 8 GPUs, which is 50 GB/s per machine. Part of what crosses it is small. DeepSeek’s model has some layers with sliding-window attention (SWA), which looks back over only a fixed number of recent tokens, so the stored cache for those layers is a fixed 20 layers × 134 tokens × 528 bytes, about 1.4 MB per sequence, whatever the prompt length. The main block cache grows with the prompt, and the time to move it adds to time to first token unless it overlaps with other work.

The Q&A is careful about which steps of a cache hit can overlap. Matching a prefix is a lookup over a chain of hashes of the token blocks, and because its result decides which machine the request goes to, the request has to wait for it. Fetching the matched blocks from storage into host memory runs asynchronously in another process. Copying them into GPU memory runs layer by layer alongside the forward pass, using RDMA network cards, which write directly into memory so the copy does not occupy the GPU’s compute units. That leaves the prefix lookup as the part of a hit that adds directly to latency.
levels.3:
Disaggregation came from a measured interference problem.

The serving loop that engines use today goes back to Orca, by Gyeong-In Yu and colleagues (OSDI 2022), which scheduled one model iteration at a time so that requests could join and leave a running batch. vLLM, from Woosuk Kwon and colleagues (SOSP 2023), then stored the attention cache in fixed-size pages so those batches could stay large without fragmenting memory (see the PagedAttention paper). DeepInfer descends from it directly, and twenty-one files in its Python package carry a header saying they were derived from vLLM.

Putting prefill and decode in the same batch has a cost, because a long prompt can stall every decoding request that shares its step. DistServe, by Yinmin Zhong and colleagues (OSDI 2024), measured that interference and proposed separate prefill and decode instances. It also changed what gets measured, to goodput: the highest request rate at which a target fraction of requests meet both a time-to-first-token target and a per-token latency target. Splitwise, by Pratyush Patel and colleagues at Microsoft (ISCA 2024), went on to put the two phases on different pools of machines and asked whether each pool should use different hardware.

Engines that keep both phases on one machine improved in the meantime. Sarathi-Serve, by Amey Agrawal and colleagues (OSDI 2024), introduced chunked prefill, which cuts prompts into chunks and mixes them with decode work so that no single step stalls for long, and DeepInfer’s prefill path does a version of this. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production describes a cost model, a quadratic curve fitted to measured step times, that picks each chunk’s size to fill a per-step time budget. So the comparison a new deployment should make is between disaggregated serving and a well-tuned single-machine engine with chunked prefill, by goodput on its own traffic, since either system’s peak throughput says little about that choice.

DeepSeek’s production numbers describe one operating point.

The Q&A reports that a single DeepSeek cluster serves 155 trillion tokens a day and earns US$38 per GPU-hour at off-peak prices, and that its load balancers reach about 80% of the throughput of a perfectly balanced offline benchmark. These are DeepSeek’s own figures, not reproduced here, and they come from a design whose smallest efficient unit is 64 prefill GPUs plus 64 decode GPUs, with each decode instance spread across 64 to 128 GPUs using wide expert parallelism. They tell you a lot about running at that scale and little about an eight-GPU deployment.

Several of DeepSeek’s choices also lean on its model. Prefill and decode can sit in different but adjacent data centers because DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, the model DeepInfer serves, compresses its attention cache heavily, so the state sent between buildings is small. The router can ignore prefix affinity, the usual practice of sending a request to the machine that already holds its prefix, because every prefill machine reads from a shared storage cluster and can find any prefix there. A system whose cache lives on the GPU that computed it faces the opposite trade, since routing requests toward their prefix can overload the machine that holds a popular one.

Failure handling is part of the architecture.

The Q&A accepts that restarts take minutes and gets reliability from spare capacity and rerouting instead of faster restarts. A decode engine that receives a shutdown notice gets a one-minute grace period and then forwards its unfinished requests, with their caches, to other decode engines. The platform will not scale in while quota utilization is above 0.8. And because a large expert-parallel instance forms one communication domain, a single failed GPU takes down the whole instance, which on restart is rebuilt at whatever expert-parallel size the healthy GPUs allow. Llumnix, by Biao Sun and colleagues (OSDI 2024), studied migrating running requests between instances as a general scheduling tool, and DeepSeek’s forwarding at shutdown is a narrower use of the same ability.

How long to keep cached prefixes turns out to be an economic choice with measured costs. The Q&A keeps them three days for agent traffic and seven for chatbot traffic, and reports that cutting chatbot traffic to three days would cost 0.5 to 1 percentage point of hit rate, because a small number of chatbot prefixes keep being read over a long period.

Problems this design leaves open.

When models and adapters change under a running fleet, cache keys have to include the model and adapter identity, or a request can read attention state computed by a different model. Balancing load means weighing how many requests a machine holds against their total cache length, and the Q&A says its decode balancer does this by rule of thumb. Published systems also rarely report goodput under bursty arrivals, which is exactly when queue policy has the largest effect on users.

LESSONS.title: Read DeepInfer without getting lost
LESSONS.goal: How one request travels through DeepInfer’s code, from the offline example script to the outputs it returns.
LESSONS.recall: What evidence separates an engine feature from a production service feature?
LESSONS.predict: Will reading every kernel before the request loop give you the clearest first map?
example: You find an output clone inside the generation loop. How do you decide whether it is needed?

The first thing to learn is what the raw output points to. Here, the nearby code and comment concern storage that a later engine step can release or reuse. Appending the object to a list would only keep a reference to that storage, and the contents behind a reference can change.
Next comes timing. If the consumer can read the saved result after the producer has overwritten the buffer behind it, the copy is what keeps the two lifetimes apart.

A test can settle the question before anyone removes the copy. It saves one output, forces the engine to reuse the buffer, and reads the saved output again. Any replacement has to keep that earlier value intact, either by copying or by handing ownership of the buffer to the caller in a way the test can check.

questions.prompt: What is the best first route through the repository?
options: Start with an example and follow one request through to its results.
Read every file in directory order, so nothing is missed, before tracing a request.
Start from the most optimized kernels, since they dominate the benchmark results.
questions.why: Following one request ties every file you open to behavior you can observe, so the map you build stays connected.
questions.hint: Which route connects each file you open to something you can watch happen?
option_feedback: Right. One traced request shows how the pieces cooperate, and each file answers part of a question you already have.
Reading in directory order covers files without showing how they connect, so the details rarely add up to a map.
Kernels decide speed, but without the request loop you cannot tell when they run or what they receive.

questions.prompt: DeepInfer’s confidence scheduler (schedule_mtp_varlen.py) ranks each draft position by the running product of the confidences up to it, not by that position’s own confidence. Why?
options: Products are cheaper to compute on a GPU than individual confidences
A position is useful only if every earlier draft in the sequence is also accepted, and the running product estimates that joint chance
The running product makes later positions rank higher, so longer drafts get verified
questions.why: Verification stops at the first rejected draft, so a position contributes only when all the positions before it survive. The product estimates that chance, and because it can never increase along a draft, the positions a sequence wins always form a prefix.
questions.hint: What happens to the later drafts when an earlier one is rejected?
option_feedback: The scheduler computes the confidences either way. The product is used because of what it means.
Right. The product is the estimated chance that the whole prefix up to that position survives.
A product of numbers no greater than 1 can only fall along the draft, so later positions rank lower.

questions.prompt: An output is cloned just before the engine may reuse its buffers. What should you check before calling the clone waste?
options: Whether a saved result would change after the buffer is reused
Whether the optimizer state is updated during inference
Whether the clone makes the output tensor larger
questions.why: If the consumer reads after the producer has overwritten the buffer, removing the copy lets it read changed data.
questions.hint: When can the engine reuse the buffer, and when is the saved result read?
option_feedback: Right. The clone may be what keeps the saved result’s lifetime separate from the reused buffer’s.
Inference does not run an optimizer, so optimizer state cannot explain a copy in the generation loop.
A clone has the same shape and size as its source. What matters is whether its values stay fixed.

transfer: Trace one request through DeepInfer in a few sentences. Name one property you would test at a specific boundary.
Traces entrypoint to scheduling to execution to sampling
Names request-owned state
Names an observable invariant

The example creates the model and calls generation. The entry point admits the requests, then repeatedly asks the engine to schedule and execute work. Model execution produces the values that sampling uses, and result handling updates each request and collects its outputs. Each request keeps its own state. At the output-collection boundary, I would test that an output saved earlier stays unchanged after a later step reuses the producer’s buffer.
LESSONS.takeaway: In DeepInfer a request goes from LLM.generate through the C++ scheduler, asynchronous model execution and sampling, and each output is cloned because its pooled storage is reused one step later.

levels.1:
You can understand one path through a repository before you understand every file.

Opening a large engine repository can feel like walking into the middle of a conversation. There are kernels, the GPU programs that do the arithmetic, along with worker processes, configuration flags and several different objects that each represent a request, and reading the files in alphabetical order rarely shows how they cooperate.

It works better to start from one concrete question, such as what happens when an example script asks the model for a response. If you follow that request from input to output, each function you meet answers a smaller part of the question you already have.

The example script shows the inputs.

A natural starting point is the offline example, examples/offline_inference.py, a short script that loads the model and generates text for a few prompts. It chooses a model, sets how many devices take part, creates the engine and asks for outputs. Most of its options can wait; what you want from it first is what it passes into generation and what it expects back.

The public entry point admits requests and collects results.

The object the example creates is the LLM class in deepinfer/entrypoints/llm.py, whose generation method admits requests and then loops until they finish. Following the call that adds a request, and then the loop that collects its outputs, shows where each request’s identity comes from, which state belongs to it, and how results come back in the right order. These are the engine responsibilities from earlier topics, now visible in code.

One engine step schedules, executes and post-processes.

That loop drives the engine in deepinfer/engine/llm_engine.py. Each call to its step method asks the scheduler which work to run, starts model execution, which proceeds asynchronously on the GPU, and then handles the results by updating each request’s state. Once you have traced that sequence, the kernels are much easier to place when you open them later.

One detail is enough for a first investigation.

A good first detail sits in the entry point itself, where output objects are cloned before the next step can reuse their underlying storage. A copy in a loop that runs every step looks like an easy saving, but the comment beside it ties the copy to storage that a later step reuses, which makes it a clue about how long data lives.

Sampling, in sampler.py, is another good choice, because it keeps ordinary token selection next to the code that verifies draft tokens from speculative decoding. Whichever detail you pick, what you want to pin down is the inputs it receives and the outputs it owns.

It also helps to mark each line of your notes as something you saw in the code, something the authors report, or something you inferred. The source links in this course point to one fixed commit, so a colleague can open exactly the code you read.
levels.2:
From the caller to the engine.

LLM.generate in deepinfer/entrypoints/llm.py accepts either text prompts or prompt_token_ids, along with one SamplingParams object or a list of them, and calls _add_request for each prompt. That function deep-copies the sampling parameters so that one request’s bookkeeping cannot leak into another’s, draws a string request ID from a counter, and, when it is given text, calls tokenizer.encode directly. No chat template is applied anywhere on this path, so laying a conversation out in the format the model was trained on is the caller’s job. The resulting IDs become a one-dimensional np.int32 array.

LLMEngine.add_request wraps those IDs in a Sequence and, for most requests, passes it straight to scheduler.add_sequence. A request with a structured-output schema waits instead while its grammar compiles asynchronously, and a callback enqueues it once the compiled matcher is ready.

The loop and its lockstep condition.

_run_engine keeps going while any request is unfinished, but the way it decides that is worth noticing. has_unfinished_requests answers with an all-reduce, a collective operation in which every rank contributes a value and gets back the combined result, here the maximum across the data-parallel group. So every rank keeps stepping until the last one is done, because the expert-parallel communication inside the model needs every participant, even a rank with nothing left to run.

Each step calls the C++ scheduler, which returns a list of SequenceMetadata and a SchedulerOutputs record saying whether this is a prompt step, which sequences were scheduled or finished, and which cache blocks to clone. Blocks are cloned when a request forks from a shared prefix and must not write into blocks another request is still reading. _execute_model_async_step then asks the workers to run execute_model_step and returns an array of uint64 handles to output objects.

Outputs arrive one step late and expire one step later.

With zero-overhead scheduling on, which is the default for normal engines, the CPU schedules step N+1 while the GPU is still running step N. The docstring of process_output spells out the consequence, which is that the outputs handled during a step belong to the previous one. When no work remains, the loop calls flush_inflight_reqs once to collect the step still in flight, and only then stops.

The output handles point into a RequestOutputPool, and the step docstring says they are released automatically at the next step. The DeferredRelease class does that during the following pre_sampler_sync, overlapped with GPU work. This is why _run_engine calls RequestOutput.clone on every raw output before appending it to a list, since without the clone the list would hold handles to pooled objects that a later step reuses. At the end the results are sorted by integer request ID. With the default decode_sequence=True the caller gets decoded strings, while the examples pass False to keep per-token objects with log-probabilities and draft statistics.

A small kernel worth checking by hand.

The confidence scheduler, schedule_mtp_varlen.py, decides how many of each sequence’s draft tokens the target model verifies in a step. It receives each sequence’s confidence for its draft positions and a total query budget total_q. In its first phase it turns each sequence’s confidences into running products, which estimate the chance that every draft up to that position is accepted, using 0 for a sequence that has no previous step. In the second it ranks every (sequence, position) pair against all the others. Each sequence gets one mandatory slot for the target model’s own token, plus one more for each of its positions that ranks inside the remaining total_q − num_seqs.

A small case makes this concrete. With two sequences of three drafts each and total_q = 5, there are 3 extra slots to hand out. Sequence A has confidences 0.9, 0.8 and 0.5, so its running products are 0.9, 0.72 and 0.36, and sequence B has 0.6, 0.9 and 0.9, giving 0.6, 0.54 and 0.486. The three largest products are A’s 0.9 and 0.72 and B’s 0.6, so A verifies 1 + 2 = 3 positions and B verifies 1 + 1 = 2. Because a running product of numbers no greater than 1 can only fall, and ties go to the lower flat index, the positions a sequence wins always form a prefix of its draft, which is what verification needs, since it stops at the first rejected draft.

Many comments in the repository are in Chinese. Machine translation handles them well, and they often state the invariant the code depends on, as the DeferredRelease docstring does.
levels.3:
The tests show what the authors promise.

Function names tell you what code is responsible for, but the tests under tests/models show which properties DeepSeek thought worth checking on real hardware, and how strictly.

  • test_offline_inference.py compares decode perplexities, a measure of how well the model predicts the text, sample by sample against exact stored baselines in offline_decode_ppl.json, keyed by platform and workload. The examples README describes a separate script that refreshes those baselines once a numerical change has been confirmed as intended.
  • test_batch_invariant.py runs the same prompts batched and one at a time with DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 and requires identical tokens and log-probabilities.
  • test_kl.py decodes long image-and-text prompts, appends the generated tokens to the prompt, recomputes everything in one prefill, and bounds the KL divergence, a measure of how far one probability distribution is from another, between the two sets of log-probabilities. For the case in the file the bound is 0.
  • test_sampler.py checks that sampled tokens follow the intended distribution, using a randomized probability integral transform and a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, for greedy sampling and several temperature and top-p settings.

Between them, the tests cover bit-for-bit reproducibility under a flag, agreement between two execution paths, and the statistical correctness of sampling, so a change that touches one path should say which of these it preserves.

A candidate change has to keep the lifetime contract.

The output clone in _run_engine is a good example of judging a change. A profiler shows a copy on every step, and it looks removable, but step returns pooled objects that DeferredRelease frees one step later precisely so the caller has time to read them. Removing the clone safely means replacing that arrangement, for instance by consuming outputs before the next step or by explicitly giving the caller ownership of the pooled object. A test that saves one output, runs another step and reads the saved output again can tell the safe design from the unsafe one, which comparing shapes never could.

The confidence scheduler invites the same reasoning. A useful contribution would be a plain Python reference for it, with running products, a global ranking with ties broken by flat index, and one mandatory slot per sequence, against which the kernel is compared over random confidences, fresh sequences, ties, and budgets at both extremes, from total_q equal to the number of sequences up to every position selected. The kernel is correct when each sequence’s selection is a prefix of its draft and the selections add up to total_q, so those are the two properties the comparison should assert.

DeepInfer’s lineage, and where it departs from vLLM.

The README says DeepInfer was originally built mainly on vLLM, with ideas from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM, and 21 files in the package carry a “Derived from vLLM” header. That makes vLLM’s documentation a help with class names like LLMEngine and SamplingParams, but the resemblance stops in places that matter. DeepInfer’s scheduler has moved to C++, and its asynchronous scheduling follows an overlap design that DeepSeek’s production Q&A credits to SGLang and NanoFlow, two systems that overlap CPU scheduling, computation and communication. The release also supports only one model family on two kinds of accelerator. So what vLLM does is only a guess about what DeepInfer does until the pinned file confirms it.

Some changes are also the wrong size for this repository. The README lists what the release leaves out, namely the cache storage system, disaggregated serving and load balancing, so a pull request adding an online server or a new model architecture raises a design question for the maintainers before anyone reviews the patch. (CONTRIBUTING.md covers formatting and test conventions and says nothing about scope.) A corrected benchmark, a reference test for an existing kernel or a fixed lifetime bug can be judged on its evidence alone.

None of these tests can run without the target hardware. Every one needs SM100 GPUs (NVIDIA’s Blackwell data-center generation) or Huawei Ascend NPUs, plus the full checkpoint. A CPU-runnable reference for small kernels like the confidence scheduler would let far more people check changes, and until one exists, a claim that such a kernel is correct rests on tests few readers can run.

levels.1:
A weights file is only part of the model you trained.

Suppose you fine-tune a base model and want to run the result in an inference engine. It is tempting to think a weights file finishes the job, but the engine also has to know what those numbers mean and how inputs were represented while the model learned them.

It starts with the model’s architecture, the arrangement of layers and calculations that its configuration file describes, which the engine has to support. Fine-tuning changes the learned numbers inside that arrangement and leaves the arrangement itself alone, so an engine that cannot run the base model cannot run your tuned version either.

An adapter may contain only the change.

With LoRA, a common fine-tuning method, what you train is a compact update attached to selected matrices of the base model. The saved adapter usually leaves out the base weights themselves, so running it takes the compatible base as well as the adapter’s configuration and learned values.

“Compatible” is stricter than it sounds. Two revisions of a base model can share every dimension and still hold different learned numbers, so an adapter trained on one may load onto the other without a shape error, and the clean load says nothing about whether it now computes what you trained.

The text format is part of what the model learned.

Before the model sees anything, a tokenizer assigns IDs to pieces of text and to special markers. For a chat-trained model, a chat template first arranges messages and roles into the token sequence the model expects, while a completion model may expect whatever custom format you used during training.

Change any of these and behavior can shift while every weight loads cleanly, which is why the intended tokenizer, input format and stop-token rules belong with the model files.

Enough to rebuild the same computation.

The practical answer is an artifact manifest, a short record of the pieces you used: the exact base revision, the adapter or merged weights, the model configuration, the tokenizer and format, the numerical precision and the relevant library versions. It records a revision that cannot change, because a name like “latest base” points somewhere new every time the base is updated.

You can serve an adapter next to its base or, where the tooling allows, merge its update into a full set of weights. Each route needs its own checks, especially once reduced precision or quantization is involved.

Before any optimization, it pays to load the intended combination in a reference implementation and save a few fixed inputs with their expected scores or task results, so that when an engine later appears to run the model you have something concrete to compare against.
levels.2:
What a LoRA adapter stores.

LoRA leaves each targeted weight matrix W frozen and learns two thin matrices beside it, B with as many rows as W and r columns, and A with r rows and as many columns as W. The adapted weight is W′ = W + s·BA, where r is the rank and s a scaling factor. B starts at zero, so training begins exactly at the base model. Because r is small next to the dimensions of W, the adapter file is a small fraction of the model, and the base matrices it modifies are not in it at all. That is why the adapter is useless without the exact base it was trained against.

The configuration decides what the numbers mean.

Hugging Face’s PEFT library, the usual tool for training LoRA adapters, saves an adapter as a directory that usually holds adapter_config.json and adapter_model.safetensors (see the PEFT LoRA reference). The second file uses the safetensors format, which stores named tensors, and the first records the base model’s name, the rank r, lora_alpha, the target_modules the update attaches to, and variant flags. Those flags change the scale. Ordinary LoRA uses s = lora_alpha / r, while the rank-stabilized variant, switched on by use_rslora, uses s = lora_alpha / √r.

So a loader that ignores a flag fails silently. With r = 16 and lora_alpha = 32, ordinary scaling gives s = 2 and rank-stabilized scaling gives s = 8, so a loader that drops the rsLoRA flag applies a quarter of the trained update while every shape still matches. Errors in the other direction behave differently. The tensor names inside the safetensors file encode module paths, so a base with renamed modules fails loudly, whereas a base with the same names but a different revision loads cleanly with different values underneath.

Merged and unmerged routes compute the same thing differently.

For an input row x, the unmerged route computes xWᵀ + s·(xAᵀ)Bᵀ, paying a little extra work on every token for each adapted matrix. The merged route folds s·BA into W once and then costs nothing extra, but the result is a full checkpoint tied to one adapter. Keeping adapters unmerged lets one copy of the base serve many of them, and vLLM’s adapter serving does this per request. In exact arithmetic the two routes agree, but in BF16 they round at different points, so their outputs can differ in the last digits. A wrong scale or a skipped target module looks different from that rounding noise, because it shifts results systematically and moves task scores.

Serving many adapters on one base also has a consequence for caching. An adapter attached to the key and value projections changes the attention cache for every token, so a prefix cache keyed on token IDs alone could hand one adapter’s cached state to a request running another. Adapter identity has to be part of the cache key.

Text becomes IDs through two separate artifacts.

The tokenizer maps strings to IDs, and the chat template decides which strings the tokenizer sees. For Hugging Face models the template is stored as a Jinja template in tokenizer_config.json, and calling apply_chat_template(messages, add_generation_prompt=True) appends the header that tells a chat model its turn has begun. Leave that out and the model sees a different sequence. The Transformers documentation on chat templates also warns that templated text already contains its special tokens, so tokenizing it again with add_special_tokens=True can duplicate a beginning-of-sequence token.

What DeepInfer does with each artifact.

The LLM constructor in deepinfer/entrypoints/llm.py takes model, tokenizer, revision and tokenizer_revision, so a pinned commit can be passed for both. But _add_request calls tokenizer.encode on raw text and applies no template, and the offline examples use plain few-shot completion prompts. DeepSeek’s chat formatting lives in a separate component, DeepSeek Recipe, which DeepSeek’s production Q&A describes as converting API requests into token sequences. It encodes strings such as <｜User｜> that appear inside user text as ordinary tokens, so pasted text cannot inject control tokens.

The release supports one model family and has no adapter loader. Searching the package for LoRA finds only kv_lora_rank, the compressed attention dimension of DeepSeek’s multi-head latent attention, which is a low-rank projection built into the architecture and has nothing to do with fine-tuning adapters despite the name.

Since each artifact feeds the next, checks go in pipeline order: the configuration and module names first, then token IDs for fixed strings, then logits on fixed IDs, and finally task behavior.

levels.1:
The code above is the cache read from a tiny engine. A cache lets the engine skip recomputing earlier tokens, but attention still has to read every piece of history it needs, and a one-line change to this read can drop part of that history without changing the length of any array.

What a slice selects.

Python counts positions from zero, and the colon in a slice means “from here to the end,” so with two saved entries [0:] selects positions 0 and 1 while [1:] selects only position 1. The stored arrays keep their full size either way. The slice only decides which entries the calculation receives.

What each entry stores.

Each saved entry holds a key and a value, two vectors of numbers computed from a token and its position. The current token supplies the query, named q in the code, and attention compares it with each visible key, then uses the resulting weights to mix the matching values.

Leave an entry out of the read and its contribution to that mixture disappears. The rest of the model then works from a different mixture and produces different next-token scores, even though the key and value slices still have equal lengths.

Where the scores first change.

Nothing goes wrong while the cache holds a single entry, so the difference first appears when the second input arrives. “See an example” shows the actual entries and attention weights at each position, and “Try it” lets you change the highlighted value, predict which entries remain, run your version, and then explain why your repair is justified.

The model behind the lab uses random weights and numbered tokens, so its output will never read as fluent language. Its purpose is to make each step of the calculation visible.
levels.2:
The tiny engine’s shapes.

The lab’s model, tiny_engine.py, is a single transformer block with random weights: width 12, a vocabulary of 16 token IDs, one attention head, learned position vectors, a residual connection and a small tanh MLP. input_vector adds a token’s 12-number embedding to its position’s 12-number vector, and three 12 × 12 matrices turn that input into a query, a key and a value. After n tokens, then, the cache holds n keys and n values of 12 numbers each.

From there attention_weights scores each visible key against the query as a dot product divided by √12 and applies softmax, which gives one weight per visible position with the weights summing to 1. attention returns the weighted sum of the visible values, again 12 numbers, and finish_block applies the output projection, the residual, a 24-wide hidden layer and the projection back. Finally output_logits multiplies by a 16 × 12 output matrix to produce 16 next-token scores.

Two paths to the same scores.

The reference, full_logits, recomputes the query, key and value at every position of a prefix and lets position i attend to positions 0 through i. Producing scores for each new token this way repeats all the earlier work, which is exactly what a cache exists to avoid. cached_step computes the query, key and value for the new token only, appends the key and value to the cache, and attends over the stored lists.

Because both paths perform the same scalar operations on the same numbers in the same order, the lab can demand agreement to within 10⁻¹⁰. A vectorized port would sum in a different order, and its tolerance would then have to allow for double-precision rounding over that many additions.

Where the broken read first shows up.

With broken_offset on, the read starts at 1 once the cache holds more than one entry. On the lesson’s prompt, token IDs 1, 4, 2, 8, the scores match exactly at prefix length 1, because the cache has one entry and the condition is false. At length 2 the reference splits attention between positions 0 and 1, while the broken read sees only position 1 and gives it weight 1.0, and the largest score difference is about 0.165. Position 0 stays missing at lengths 3 and 4, where the differences are about 0.097 and 0.059. They shrink because each new entry dilutes the missing one’s share of attention, but every later step is still computed without position 0.

Watching the generated text would be a weaker check. The highest-scoring token can survive a 0.165 shift in some scores, so a broken cache can keep producing the right next token for a while, whereas comparing all 16 scores at every position catches the error at the first prefix where it exists.

What the reference checks cover.

The “Try it” panel runs reference_checks, which reports 218 comparisons. Most of them, 177, compare cached and full-prefix scores after every position for three random seeds and prompt lengths 1, 2, 7, 16 and 33. Another 15 compare six-token greedy continuations. Two interleaved requests with separate caches are each compared to their own reference, 24 comparisons that would catch a cache shared by mistake. One hand-built rank-2 update to the output matrix is applied both separately and merged into the weights, the only adapter-like case, since the tiny engine loads no trained adapters. The last check confirms that a model with a maximum context of 2 rejects a third token without appending it to the cache.

A scheduler extension would be tested the same way, by comparing each request against its own independent generation, including requests that finish early and a new request that takes over a freed slot.
levels.3:
The same oracle runs in DeepInfer’s test suite.

The comparison you ran in the lab, cached decoding against a full recomputation, is also how DeepInfer’s tests/models/test_kl.py checks the production engine, using it as an oracle at far larger scale. The test builds image-and-text prompts of 16,384 tokens and decodes 1,024 tokens per prompt, forcing the tokens to a fixed golden sequence so the run does not depend on sampling. It then appends the generated tokens to the prompt, runs the whole sequence again as one prefill, and asks for the log-probability of every token. Two assertions follow: the prompt log-probabilities must be identical across the two runs, and the KL divergence between decode-time and prefill-time log-probabilities must not exceed max_kl, which is 0 for the case in the file. The run uses speculative drafting, context parallelism and expert parallelism over 8 GPUs, with DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 set.

That flag is what makes a bound of zero possible. Without batch invariance, a sum can be split differently depending on how many tokens share the batch, so a decode step and a long prefill add the same numbers in different orders and round differently. Horace He and colleagues at Thinking Machines Lab described this source of nondeterminism in 2025 and showed kernels that remove it. DeepInfer’s README offers batch-invariant inference on NVIDIA hardware only, and anywhere else some nonzero tolerance is unavoidable. For those cases deepinfer.testing.cal_diff reports cosine difference, root-mean-square error, the largest single difference and KL divergence, which together describe both the size and the shape of a disagreement.

Two implementations can share a bug.

Checking one implementation against another is called differential testing, a name William McKeeman gave the practice in 1998, and the tiny engine shows where it is weak. full_logits and cached_step call the same input_vector, attention and finish_block, so a wrong scaling factor inside attention would appear in both paths and pass every comparison. The cache-offset bug is caught only because it lives in the one line the two paths do not share.

Covering that gap takes checks that do not route through shared code. A hand-computed case with two positions and tiny integer weights tests the arithmetic directly. Invariants catch whole classes of error, for instance that attention weights sum to 1 and that the scores for a prefix do not depend on tokens after it. A metamorphic test changes something that should not matter, such as which other request shares the batch, and requires the output to stay the same, which is what the lab’s interleaved-request check does.

Keeping the oracle as the engine grows.

Each natural extension of the tiny engine changes one mechanism and comes with its own test. A NumPy or PyTorch port of the arithmetic keeps the scalar version as the oracle, with a tolerance chosen for the new summation order. Continuous admission with two active slots keeps the caches separate and compares every request with its independent generation, including early finishes and slot reuse. Paged storage needs tests at lengths of one page minus one, exactly one page and one page plus one, along with page reuse, and an explicit maximum-context policy, reject or truncate, needs a test of its own, since silently changing what attention sees changes behavior.

DeepInfer’s KL test needs eight GPUs and the full checkpoint, while the tiny engine runs in milliseconds on a laptop and can be rerun after every change.

You want two things from a first deployment: that it runs the model you actually trained, and that it runs it efficiently. The first has to be settled before speed can justify any change, because if you change both at once and the output differs, you cannot tell whether the model files, the input format, the numerical format or the engine caused it.

The engine has to support the model’s calculations.

So the starting point is the exact architecture and configuration of your base model, which the engine has to support along with the adapter path you use and the numerical format you plan to serve. vLLM’s list of supported models is one place to look this up, since vLLM is a widely used open-source engine that covers many architectures.

DeepInfer, the advanced case study in this course, is built around DeepSeek’s own models and makes no promise to run every model fine-tuned from every base. A compatible general-purpose engine is usually the more practical first home for your model.

Fixed inputs.

Using the correct tokenizer and the training-time format, you turn your test prompts into prompt IDs and record them with the stop rules and generation settings. All of that stays fixed whenever the reference and the engine are compared.

Fixing the IDs, and not just the visible text, avoids a common confusion, because two systems can show the same question on screen and still run different token sequences if each formatted it differently.

The model is checked before an API goes around it.

The first run loads the intended base plus adapter, or the intended merged checkpoint, in a direct reference implementation. It saves numerical predictions where possible and scores examples from a held-out set, cases kept out of training that show how the model behaves beyond the examples it was fitted to.

The compatible engine then runs on the same inputs. The strongest comparison is next-token probabilities, where the engine exposes them, followed by greedy outputs under controlled settings and then the task results you care about. When only the weaker comparisons are available, your notes should say so.

Complexity comes one change at a time.

Once offline generation matches, a local endpoint comes next, then concurrent requests, and after that tests of limits, cancellation, a range of input lengths and reloading. Quantization is an experiment of its own, so that any change in quality has one identifiable cause.

An HTTP 200 response tells you the endpoint answered. It cannot show that your adapter was active or that the model still behaves as it did in the reference, which is why the artifact identities and reference comparisons are kept next to the service measurements.
levels.2:
The comparison table comes before the server.

It helps to lay the first deployment out as a table with four rows: the base model in a reference implementation, the adapted model in that reference, the adapted model in the engine, and optionally a quantized engine run. Each neighboring pair differs in one thing. The gap between the first two rows is what fine-tuning changed, the gap between the second and third comes from execution, and the gap between the third and fourth comes from numerical representation.

Teacher-forced log-probabilities are the strongest comparison.

Comparing generated text has a weakness, since one early disagreement sends the two systems down different paths and every later token differs too. Teacher forcing avoids that by giving each system a fixed prompt plus a fixed continuation, for example the reference model’s greedy output, as one input, and asking for the log-probability it assigns to every token. Every position then sees identical inputs. In vLLM the prompt_logprobs field of SamplingParams returns these values for the prompt tokens, and DeepInfer’s own tests use the same pattern, with test_kl.py passing golden_token_ids to force a continuation and prompt_logprobs=True to read back the recomputed values. The useful summary is the largest and mean absolute difference per token, plus the positions where the top-ranked token changes.

When an engine exposes no log-probabilities, greedy continuations under fixed settings are the next best thing, and the first position where they diverge is what to record. A divergence at a near-tie between two tokens is weak evidence of a bug, while one at a position where the model was confident is strong evidence. Task scores on held-out data come last, because they answer a different question, whether the model still does its job, which neither of the other comparisons can.

Checking that the adapter is active.

vLLM serves adapters when started with --enable-lora and a --lora-modules entry mapping a name to an adapter path (see vLLM’s LoRA serving guide). A request selects the adapter by putting that name in its model field, and the response echoes the name back, which shows the name was accepted but not that the adapter’s numbers were applied. Held-out prompts on which the base and adapted references clearly differ settle the question. If the engine matches the base row on them, the update never took effect.

Where DeepInfer fits.

The release supports DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs, and it documents no adapter path. Even its low-precision formats were chosen together with that model. DeepSeek’s production Q&A lists 4-bit floating-point (FP4) variants for the main cache, for the smaller cache the model uses to choose which earlier tokens to attend to, and for the routed expert weights. For most fine-tuned models, then, DeepInfer is reading material, and the first deployment runs on a general engine with documented support for the architecture.

Service checks come after the table matches.

Only then is the endpoint tested under mixed prompt lengths, concurrent requests, cancellation mid-stream, requests at the context limit, and a restart or reload. After a reload the fixed inputs are run again and compared with the saved rows, since a reload is another chance to load the wrong files.

LESSONS.title: Judge a performance claim and test one change
LESSONS.goal: How to tell whether an engine change helped your workload, and how to record the evidence so that someone else can rerun it.
LESSONS.recall: Which correctness promise did your last optimization actually make?
LESSONS.predict: A chart says 2× faster. What would you need to know to decide whether that helps your workload?
example: DeepInfer’s README reports decode throughput from its benchmark script. Before comparing that figure with your own deployment, what does it actually count?

The script computes decode throughput as steps per second × requests × (1 + draft length). Each request is credited with the target’s own token plus every draft token at every step, 6 tokens at the default draft length of 5, whatever fraction of drafts the target accepted. The README calls this full-acceptance accounting, so the figure is an upper bound.

Real acceptance is lower. DeepSeek’s production Q&A reports accepted lengths of about 3.1 to 3.3 tokens for 5-token drafts, and acceptance on your fine-tuned model and traffic could differ again. The plotting script can rescale results by an assumed acceptance rate, and it refuses to do so for runs whose step counts already reflect acceptance.

The benchmark also measures steady state with every request present from the start, after warmup and with profiling off. It says nothing about queueing under real arrivals. Comparing it with your deployment means measuring accepted tokens, latency percentiles and arrivals on your own workload under the same accounting.

questions.prompt: The authors’ benchmark shows a 2× speedup. Can you expect the same speedup for your deployment?
options: Yes, because the engine code is the same
No, because the workload and configuration limit what the result shows
Yes, as long as your cluster is at least as large as theirs
questions.why: A benchmark is evidence about the conditions it measured. Your request lengths, arrivals, precision and cache state may differ.
questions.hint: What variables were held fixed?
option_feedback: The same code can behave very differently under other request lengths, batch sizes or cache states.
Right. The speedup belongs to the measured workload and configuration until you reproduce it under yours.
Hardware is only one condition, and a different workload on equal hardware can still lose the gain.

questions.prompt: A: 2,000 tok/s, p99 ITL 180 ms. B: 1,600 tok/s, p99 60 ms. Limit 80 ms. Choose…
options: A, because its throughput is higher
B, among these measured configurations
Either, since p99 describes only the slowest 1% of gaps
questions.why: A’s 180 ms p99 gap breaks the 80 ms limit and B’s 60 ms meets it, so B is the only configuration that qualifies.
questions.hint: Which configurations meet the 80 ms limit at all?
option_feedback: Higher throughput counts only among configurations that already meet the latency requirement, and A misses it.
Right. After filtering by the 80 ms requirement, B is the only one left.
The requirement is stated as a p99 limit, so the slowest 1% of gaps is exactly what it constrains.

questions.prompt: A write-up says confidence-scheduled verification raised throughput 5% and cites DeepSeek’s production Q&A. What is the most important thing to check before relying on it?
options: The concurrency it applies at, since the Q&A’s estimates run from −1.5% at 16 sequences per rank to +11% at 96
Whether the 5% was measured with the profiler on, since profiling only adds noise and the mean is unaffected
Nothing further, since the gain came from the engine’s authors on production hardware
questions.why: The Q&A’s figures are estimates whose sign and size depend on how many sequences each GPU is decoding. A 5% gain belongs to one load, and yours may sit elsewhere on the curve.
questions.hint: Did the Q&A report one number or a curve?
option_feedback: Right. The gain turns into a loss at low concurrency, so the load decides whether the claim applies to you.
Profiling does distort results, but it inflates step times in one direction, so it is not zero-mean noise, and the Q&A figures came from benchmark data in any case.
Author-reported figures are evidence about the authors’ workload, and the Q&A’s own table shows the result depends on load.

transfer: Choose one DeepInfer idea and explain whether you would adopt it for your own model. What evidence would you need?
Names saved resource and new cost
States architectural and hardware assumptions
Defines a correctness oracle and matched benchmark

For confidence-based draft scheduling, I would first check that my model and engine support the drafting and verification path it needs. I would measure the acceptance rate and the cost of verification under my target request load. I would keep the intended sampling behavior, confirmed by reference checks, and compare useful throughput at matched latency and quality targets. I would adopt the mechanism only if those measurements show a worthwhile gain for that workload.
LESSONS.takeaway: A speed claim can be judged only with its baseline, workload, latency metric, correctness promise and measurement method, and DeepSeek’s own estimate for confidence-scheduled verification changes sign with the number of sequences per GPU.

activity.title: Make one change and decide what the evidence supports.
activity.intro: Use your own model experiment if you have one. Until then, write a proposed experiment and label every unmeasured result “not measured.” Choose one mechanism from the course; you can start applying it without a separate final project.

fields.label: What one change will you try, and why?
